findings.title: User-entered reminder title and detail are stored in cleartext
findings.description: The reminders table stores `title` and `detail` as plain TEXT, and repo.create_reminder (identilock/repo.py:572) inserts user-typed free text into them unencrypted. The reminders form (templates/reminders.html, fields 'What' and 'Detail') gives no hint these are different from every other free-text field, and the db.py docstring explicitly claims 'free-text notes' are encrypted — only the never-exposed notes_enc column actually is. The built-in seeded reminders are generic templates, so this leaks nothing by default, but any custom reminder leaks verbatim.
findings.failure_scenario: A user creates a reminder 'Thaw Experian for Sarah before closing — PIN 4821' or 'Renew ChexSystems freeze for Danny Arvan'. The laptop (or a synced backup of identilock.db) is stolen. `strings identilock.db` prints the child's name and the freeze PIN in the clear, despite the backup UI telling the user the file 'is encrypted with the same passphrase ... useless without it'.
findings.fix: Add title_enc/detail_enc BLOB columns via _ensure_column, register them in ENCRYPTED_FIELDS, encrypt in create_reminder/list_reminders through the vault (the only SQL ordering used is due_date, which stays cleartext), and migrate existing plaintext rows on first unlock. At minimum, until then, the reminders form must state that these two fields are stored unencrypted.

findings.title: Uploaded credit-report filename (source_name) stored in cleartext
findings.description: reports.source_name is plain TEXT and save_report (identilock/repo.py:635) stores upload.filename into it unencrypted, while the report's text and extracted entities are carefully encrypted right next to it. Credit-report downloads are routinely named after the person by the bureau or the user (e.g. 'Experian_John_Q_Public_2026-01-15.pdf').
findings.failure_scenario: User uploads 'Equifax report - Sarah Arvan 2026.pdf'. A thief with only the database file reads the filename in the clear and now knows a household member's full name and which bureau files exist for her — exactly the identity linkage the encrypted-name design says a stolen file must not reveal ('learns no identities', db.py docstring).
findings.fix: Encrypt the filename: make it source_name_enc, add it to ENCRYPTED_FIELDS, and seal it in save_report / open it in _row_to_report. Alternatively stop storing the filename entirely (it is display-only) and keep just the extension or a user-visible generic label.

findings.title: Data written after a data-dir move is silently lost at next launch
findings.description: move_data_dir copies the database to the new folder immediately (db.backup_to at click time), writes the pointer, and then lets the running session keep writing to the OLD database. The next launch follows the pointer and opens the copy made at click time, so every change made between clicking 'move' and quitting the app is absent from the new location. The success message says the current session 'keeps using the current folder' but never says those later changes will not follow the move — and it then tells the user to delete the old folder once 'the new location works'.
findings.failure_scenario: User moves the data dir, then in the same session adds a child with SSN and records three freeze PINs, quits. Next launch opens the new folder's stale copy: the child is gone. The vault opens fine, so 'the new location works'; the user deletes the old folder as instructed and the SSN/PIN records are permanently destroyed.
findings.fix: After the copy succeeds, switch the live app to the new location in the same request: set request.app.state.settings = dataclasses.replace(settings, data_dir=target) (get_conn resolves db_path per request, so all subsequent writes land in the new folder), and run ensure_data_dir on it so the 0700 chmod applies immediately rather than at next launch. Alternatively defer the copy to shutdown/startup — but the state-swap is simpler and closes the window entirely.

findings.title: Recovery code saved as world-readable plaintext file beside the vault it opens
findings.description: recovery_code_save writes the recovery code in plaintext to ~/Desktop/Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt with default umask permissions (typically 0644), on the same machine that holds identilock.db. The stated threat model is theft of the database file; a stolen laptop yields both the vault and the credential that opens it. The file's own text and the UI do warn to move it elsewhere, but nothing enforces or follows up on that, and non-technical coworkers (the stated audience) will predictably leave it on the Desktop forever.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker clicks 'Save to a file' during setup, never moves it, and the laptop is stolen a year later. The thief opens Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt from the Desktop, runs the app against the stolen data dir, uses 'Forgot your passphrase?', and reads every SSN and PIN — the exact scenario the encryption exists to prevent. On a shared POSIX machine the 0644 file is also readable by other local users.
findings.fix: Write the file with 0600 (os.open with mode, or chmod after write). Better: keep the Desktop save but make the 'I have stored my code' acknowledgment ask whether the file has been moved off this machine, and offer a one-click delete of the Desktop copy; or prefer a print flow over a file at all.

findings.title: Corrupted ciphertext decrypts to None, indistinguishable from empty, and is destroyed on next save
findings.description: Vault.decrypt catches InvalidTag/ValueError and returns None — the same value used for 'field is empty'. The UI therefore renders an undecryptable field as blank with no warning, and repo.update_person (identilock/repo.py:144-171) unconditionally re-encrypts every column from form values, so a save writes NULL over the original blob. The crypto.py docstring promises tampering is 'an integrity nuisance rather than a disclosure', but here it is silent and, after one ordinary edit, permanent: ciphertext that would still open under the correct key (e.g. the pre-change passphrase of a mixed restore) is deleted. This also undercuts honesty priority 3 — the vault looks healthy while data is unreadable.
findings.failure_scenario: User restores an Identilock.db from a backup made before a passphrase change (a scenario crypto.py:148-149 explicitly anticipates), or one blob is bit-rotted. The person's SSN field shows as empty — no error. Later the user edits that person's phone number and clicks save; update_person writes ssn_enc = NULL. The original ciphertext, which was recoverable by re-restoring the matching backup or remembering the old passphrase, is now gone with no indication anything was ever there.
findings.fix: Make decryption failure a distinct state: have Vault.decrypt raise (or return a sentinel like Undecryptable) on InvalidTag instead of None. Render such fields as 'unreadable — wrong passphrase or corrupted data' in templates, and in update paths preserve the stored blob when the submitted value corresponds to an unreadable field rather than overwriting it with NULL.

findings.title: One undecryptable blob makes passphrase change — and therefore recovery — fail entirely
findings.description: change_passphrase calls open_sealed on every non-NULL encrypted blob; a single InvalidTag (corrupt blob, or a field carried in from a backup under another key — the exact state Vault.decrypt is written to tolerate) raises, rolls back the whole transaction, and propagates as an unhandled 500 from both /settings/passphrase (identilock/routes/settings_routes.py:207) and /recover (identilock/routes/auth.py:223). In the /recover path this means a user who supplies a CORRECT recovery code (recover_data_key has already returned a verified key) still cannot get into the vault, because recovery is implemented as change-passphrase-under-the-recovered-key. The inconsistency with decrypt's lenient behavior means a vault that reads fine day-to-day is silently un-migratable.
findings.failure_scenario: One notes_enc blob in freeze_records is corrupted on disk. The app works normally (that one field renders blank). The user forgets the passphrase, finds their printed recovery code, enters it with a new passphrase — recover_data_key returns the correct key, then change_passphrase hits InvalidTag on the bad blob, rolls back, and the route 500s. Recovery is impossible through the UI even though the key is provably correct and every other field is readable. The same corruption also permanently blocks routine passphrase changes.
findings.fix: In change_passphrase, catch InvalidTag per field and carry the unreadable blob over unchanged (it is already unreadable; re-wrapping cannot make it worse), collecting a list of (table, column, pk) that failed. Return that list so the routes can show 'passphrase changed; N fields could not be re-encrypted and remain unreadable' instead of crashing. At minimum, catch the exception in both routes and render an actionable error rather than a 500.

findings.title: Recovery re-wrap is committed separately from passphrase change, leaving a window where the recovery credential is silently destroyed
findings.description: change_passphrase commits its transaction (db.py:324), and only afterwards do the callers invoke set_recovery, which commits separately (settings_routes.py:207-209, auth.py:223-225, and setup at auth.py:89-93). Between the two commits the database contains fields and verifier under the new key but recovery_wrap still wrapping the OLD key under the OLD code. A crash, kill, or any exception in set_recovery (e.g. sqlite disk-full) in that window leaves the vault permanently in that state: the old printed code fails recover_data_key's verifier check (db.py:382) and reads as 'wrong code', and the new code was never displayed. The user's saved Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt explicitly tells them the code is replaced on passphrase change, so they believe they are covered when they are not.
findings.failure_scenario: User changes their passphrase; the process is killed (laptop battery dies, OS update reboot) after change_passphrase's commit but before set_recovery's commit — or set_recovery itself throws and the route 500s so no code is ever shown. Months later they forget the new passphrase and enter the recovery code from their printed file; it is rejected as wrong. With both credentials gone, all SSNs, PINs, and records are unrecoverable — the exact total-loss outcome the recovery system exists to prevent, with no warning that it had been disarmed.
findings.fix: Fold the recovery re-wrap into change_passphrase's single transaction: generate the new code and write recovery_salt/recovery_*/recovery_wrap (sealed under the new key) before the one commit at db.py:324, returning (new_vault, code). Callers then only display the code. Apply the same single-transaction pattern to initial setup (initialize_vault + set_recovery).

findings.title: No Host-header validation; pre-auth POST endpoints reachable from any website
findings.description: The app adds security headers but never validates the Host header (no TrustedHostMiddleware) and the pre-authentication endpoints POST /setup, POST /setup/import, POST /unlock, and POST /recover (identilock/routes/auth.py:68, 231, 290, 185) have no CSRF token, no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check, and no session requirement. Any web page the user visits can fire blind cross-origin POSTs at http://localhost:8731 (the port is a fixed default), and a DNS-rebinding page (attacker domain re-resolving to 127.0.0.1) can additionally READ responses, because nothing rejects a foreign Host header. Cookie-based auth does protect unlocked-session pages from rebinding (the session cookie is keyed to the hostname the user browsed), so the exposure is limited to the pre-auth surface — but that surface includes vault initialization and vault-file replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker installs Identilock, starts it, but hasn't completed setup yet (db not initialized). While browsing, a malicious page silently sends fetch('http://localhost:8731/setup/import', {method:'POST', mode:'no-cors', body: formDataWithAttackerDb}) or an auto-submitting form to POST /setup with an attacker-chosen passphrase. The vault is now initialized/replaced under a passphrase the user doesn't know; when they run setup they're bounced to /unlock and locked out of their own fresh install. Separately, a DNS-rebinding page can read /unlock responses and grind passphrase guesses against POST /unlock at Argon2 speed for as long as the tab is open, with no lockout ('no extra lockout needed for a service reachable only from this machine' assumes only local software can reach it — rebinding breaks that assumption).
findings.fix: In create_app, add Starlette's TrustedHostMiddleware with allowed_hosts limited to localhost, 127.0.0.1, and [::1] (extended only when IDENTILOCK_ALLOW_REMOTE=1). Additionally, for the pre-auth POSTs in routes/auth.py, reject requests whose Origin (or Sec-Fetch-Site) header is present and not same-origin — browsers always send these on cross-site POSTs, while same-origin form posts and non-browser clients pass.

findings.title: Settings' "What This App Sends Over the Internet" list is incomplete
findings.description: The authoritative-sounding list on the Settings page says the app sends "Nothing, unless you use the Breaches page" and enumerates only the password-hash-prefix and email lookups. Two other egress paths exist: (1) the Sources page "Check All Links Now" button fetches ~34 agency/government URLs (identilock/routes/dashboard.py:175); (2) saving an HIBP API key on this very Settings page immediately transmits the key to haveibeenpwned.com for verification (identilock/routes/settings_routes.py:172 -> services/hibp.py verify_key). help.html does mention the link check, but the page that presents itself as the complete egress inventory contradicts it. None of the extra traffic carries personal data, so this is an honesty gap, not a leak.
findings.failure_scenario: A privacy-conscious coworker reads Settings, concludes only the Breaches page ever touches the network, then presses "Check All Links Now" (or saves an API key) while on a monitored/metered network they specifically wanted to keep this tool invisible on — and the app makes dozens of outbound requests the UI told them wouldn't happen.
findings.fix: Amend the Settings list to add two bullets: the Sources link check ("ordinary page requests to the agency sites listed on Sources, nothing about you") and that saving an HIBP key sends the key to HIBP once to verify it.

findings.title: Link-check User-Agent announces Identilock to every agency site, contradicting UI claim
findings.description: check_links sends User-Agent "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Identilock link check)" from the user's own IP to every registry URL (credit bureaus, IRS, SSA, data brokers). The Settings page promises that agency sites "do not learn you came from a tool like this" (referrer suppression), and this module's docstring claims the requests are "the same anonymous page fetches a browser would make" — but the UA tells each site, and any intermediary, that this specific machine runs an identity-protection vault. For a family that is a breach victim, advertising "this IP runs Identilock" to ~34 third parties is exactly the metadata the referrer suppression was meant to withhold. No personal data is sent; this is tool-fingerprinting only.
findings.failure_scenario: User presses "Check All Links Now" on their home network. Every agency site, CDN, and network middlebox on the path logs their IP paired with a UA naming an identity-theft-protection vault — a signal the UI explicitly promised those sites would not receive.
findings.fix: Use a generic, current browser User-Agent string with no product token (e.g. a plain Chrome UA), or drop the custom UA entirely and soften the docstring/UI claim to match whichever is chosen.

findings.title: CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' scripts, neutralizing its XSS backstop on SSN-bearing pages
findings.description: The middleware's Content-Security-Policy includes script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'. With inline script execution allowed, the CSP provides essentially no defense-in-depth against markup injection on pages that render SSNs, freeze PINs, and uploaded credit-report text. Today Jinja autoescaping appears to be the only line of defense (I found no |safe on user data), so this is a hardening gap rather than an active leak — but the header currently gives a false sense of a second layer.
findings.failure_scenario: A future template change (or a |safe filter added to render agency notes / report text) introduces an injection point in an uploaded credit report's extracted text; because 'unsafe-inline' is allowed, the injected <script> runs and can read the SSNs on the page and exfiltrate nothing is blocked by default-src only if the attacker uses fetch to an external host — but form-action/self-exfil via same-origin state changes and DOM scraping into the page remain, and img-src data: plus navigation offer exfil paths.
findings.fix: Move the app's inline scripts into files under /static and drop 'unsafe-inline' from script-src; if some inline bootstrap is unavoidable, switch to a per-response nonce (nonce-<random>) generated in the security_headers middleware.

findings.title: /setup and /setup/import accept cross-origin POSTs, letting a web page set the vault passphrase on a fresh install
findings.description: Every session-backed POST in the app calls verify_csrf, but the three pre-session state-changing endpoints — POST /setup (line 68), POST /setup/import (line 231), and POST /recover (line 185) — take no CSRF token, and nothing anywhere validates Origin, Referer, or Sec-Fetch-Site. The SameSite=strict session cookie is irrelevant here because these endpoints need no cookie to act. Any web page can therefore drive first-run setup on http://localhost:8731 (the port is the fixed default from cli.py, and the URL cli.py opens). POST /setup is the damaging one: it calls db.initialize_vault with an attacker-chosen passphrase and returns a Set-Cookie for a live session. A cross-site response may still store a SameSite=Strict cookie; Strict only suppresses sending it from cross-site contexts, so the victim's own top-level navigation to the app carries it.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker installs Identilock; it launches and shows /setup. Before finishing, they open another tab and hit a page carrying a hidden auto-submitting form to http://localhost:8731/setup with passphrase=confirm=<attacker string>&acknowledged=1. The vault is initialized under the attacker's passphrase and the victim's browser stores the resulting session cookie. The victim switches back to Identilock, navigates to /, finds it already unlocked (no setup screen, which reads to a non-technical user as "it remembered me"), and enters the family's SSNs, DOBs, and freeze PINs. Every field is now sealed under a key the attacker derived. The moment the .db file leaves the machine by any of the app's own routes — the weekly auto-backup in backup_dir, /settings/backup, or the move file that /settings/move-kit drops on the Desktop into a synced cloud folder — the attacker decrypts all of it. The lower-effort variant is POST /setup/import with an attacker-built vault, which silently replaces the fresh database and permanently locks the user out.
findings.fix: Set a random pre-session cookie plus matching hidden token on GET /setup, GET /recover and GET /unlock, and verify it on the corresponding POSTs the same way verify_csrf does. Independently, add an app-wide middleware that rejects any non-GET/HEAD request whose Origin header is present and not the app's own origin, and whose Sec-Fetch-Site is not "same-origin" or "none" — that closes this class for all current and future endpoints rather than one at a time.

findings.title: Uploaded credit reports are written to an unencrypted OS temp file, contradicting the in-app claim
findings.description: The handler comment at lines 90-91 says "The uploaded file itself is never written to disk" and templates/reports.html:59-61 tells the user "The report never goes to the internet — Identilock keeps only the words from the file, scrambled (encrypted) into its database on this computer." Neither is true. FastAPI parses the multipart body before the handler runs, and Starlette's MultiPartParser (.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/starlette/formparsers.py:147, 230) backs every file part with SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=1024*1024). Past 1 MB the spool rolls over — CPython's SpooledTemporaryFile.rollover() creates a real tempfile.TemporaryFile in the OS temp directory and writes the buffered bytes into it — so the full plaintext PDF lands on disk in %TEMP% / $TMPDIR. Credit report PDFs are routinely well over 1 MB. The MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES check at line 73 cannot prevent this: it runs after await upload.read(), by which point the body has already been fully parsed and spooled. Note that file parts are exempt from Starlette's max_part_size limit (formparsers.py:184 applies it only when _current_part.file is None), so there is no upper bound on how much is spilled.
findings.failure_scenario: The user uploads a 3 MB Experian PDF containing their full SSN, account numbers, and address history. Starlette rolls the spool over and the entire plaintext PDF is written to the temp directory. On Windows — the stated coworker platform — tempfile.TemporaryFile is a named file in %TEMP% opened with O_TEMPORARY, so while the request runs any other process running as that user can open and read it, and after close its blocks remain on disk unwiped and trivially recoverable by forensic tooling on a machine without full-disk encryption (the default on Windows Home). The vault's whole premise — that a stolen data file yields only ciphertext — is bypassed: the plaintext was on the same disk all along, and the user was explicitly told it was not.
findings.fix: Cap the request before it is parsed: in a middleware, reject POST /reports when Content-Length exceeds MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES. Then raise the spool threshold above that cap so the body never touches disk, e.g. at app startup set starlette.formparsers.MultiPartParser.spool_max_size = MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES + 1. Alternatively read the body yourself via request.stream() with a running byte count and parse the multipart in memory. Whichever route, correct the comment at reports.py:90-91 and the user-facing hint in templates/reports.html so the claim matches the behavior.

findings.title: No Host-header validation, so a remote site can reach the loopback app via DNS rebinding
findings.description: create_app installs a security-headers middleware but never validates the Host header, and no TrustedHostMiddleware is mounted. uvicorn serves any Host. Binding to 127.0.0.1 stops direct network access but not DNS rebinding: an attacker's domain resolves to their server long enough to load a page, then re-resolves to 127.0.0.1, after which the page's JavaScript can fetch http://attacker.example:8731/ as a same-origin request and read the responses. The host-scoped session cookie limits this — it was set for 127.0.0.1/localhost and is not sent to the rebound name — but the endpoints that need no cookie are exactly the dangerous ones identified in the /setup finding, and they are now reachable from the open internet rather than only from a page the user visits.
findings.failure_scenario: The victim leaves a tab open on an attacker-controlled page while Identilock is running on a fresh install. After the rebind, the page's script POSTs to /setup with a passphrase the attacker chose and reads the response — same-origin, so the Set-Cookie is stored under the attacker's hostname and every subsequent scripted fetch carries a valid session. The attacker now has a remote, scriptable, authenticated session: GET /people, /matrix, and each /freeze/{p}/{a} return decrypted names, SSNs, DOBs, and freeze PINs directly into the attacker's JavaScript, which POSTs them to their own server. On an already-initialized vault the same channel turns POST /unlock into a remote passphrase oracle whose success or failure is readable, bounded only by Argon2id cost rather than by the machine being unreachable.
findings.fix: Add a middleware ahead of the routers that rejects any request whose Host header is not in {"127.0.0.1:<port>", "localhost:<port>", "[::1]:<port>"} (built from settings.host/settings.port), returning 421 or 403. Starlette's TrustedHostMiddleware with allowed_hosts=["127.0.0.1", "localhost", "::1"] does this in one line. This is the standard defense for a localhost-only web app holding secrets, and it also hardens the app against the /setup CSRF above.

findings.title: Move file and recovery code are both dropped on ~/Desktop with default permissions — the app violates its own warning
findings.description: make_move_kit writes the complete vault to Path.home()/"Desktop"/f"Identilock-move-{stamp}.db", and recovery_code_save (routes/auth.py:127-143) writes the plaintext recovery code to Path.home()/"Desktop"/"Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt" — the same directory. The recovery code is a full second key: db.recover_data_key unwraps the data key from it directly, no passphrase involved. So those two files side by side are the plaintext vault. The save text itself warns "keep it somewhere you trust — and not in the same place as a copy of the data file itself," which the app then contradicts by placing both in one folder. Two further problems compound it: neither file's permissions are restricted (Path.write_text and db.backup_to use the default umask, typically 0644 on POSIX) even though config.ensure_data_dir deliberately chmods the data directory to 0700; and ~/Desktop is a cloud-synced folder by default on both target platforms — macOS "Desktop & Documents" iCloud sync is on by default whenever iCloud Drive is enabled, and Windows OneDrive Known Folder Move covers the Desktop for new setups.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker clicks "Moving to a New Computer" and, on the recovery-code screen, clicks "Save to a file". Both files appear on the Desktop and OneDrive/iCloud uploads them within seconds, unprompted, to the same cloud account. Anyone who later compromises that account — credential stuffing, a shared family Apple ID, a device left signed in — downloads Identilock-move-2026-08-04.db and Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt together and reads every SSN, DOB, and freeze PIN in the household, including the children's. The user was never told this would happen; they were told the opposite. On a shared POSIX machine the 0644 mode means any other local account can read the recovery code without the cloud step at all.
findings.fix: Write both files with mode 0600 (os.open with 0o600, or write then os.chmod) to match the 0700 data directory. Do not default to the Desktop for the move file — write it into settings.data_dir (or a chosen folder) and show the user the path. Keep the recovery code and any vault copy in different directories, and say plainly in the on-screen text that the Desktop is automatically uploaded to iCloud/OneDrive on most machines so the user makes that choice deliberately.

findings.title: /setup/import buffers and writes an upload of unbounded size
findings.description: setup_import does data = await upload.read() with no size check at all, then scratch.write_bytes(data) into the data directory. Unlike /reports there is not even a post-hoc MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES test. Starlette's max_part_size does not apply to file parts (formparsers.py:184 checks it only when the part has no file), so the body is limited only by available memory and disk. Combined with the missing CSRF/Origin check on this endpoint, an unauthenticated cross-origin POST reaches it whenever the vault is uninitialized.
findings.failure_scenario: A page the user visits during first-run setup POSTs a multi-gigabyte multipart body to http://localhost:8731/setup/import. The parser spools it to the temp filesystem, upload.read() then materializes the whole thing in RAM, and scratch.write_bytes writes another full copy into the user's data directory. The process is OOM-killed or the disk fills; if it dies after write_bytes, the file identilock.import-tmp is left sitting in the data directory with no cleanup path, since the unlink at line 261 only runs on the validation-failure branch.
findings.fix: Reject the request up front when Content-Length exceeds a sane cap (a real move file is at most a few MB), and stream the upload to the scratch path in chunks with a running byte counter, aborting and unlinking once the cap is passed. Wrap the whole scratch-file lifecycle in try/finally so a partial import never leaves identilock.import-tmp behind. Apply the same Content-Length precheck to /reports so its MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES limit is enforced before the body is buffered rather than after.

findings.title: Auto-backup catches only OSError; sqlite3 errors block unlock, and failed backups poison the backup set
findings.description: _maybe_auto_backup's docstring promises 'Any failure here is swallowed: a full disk must not stop the vault from opening', but the except clause catches only OSError. db.backup_to raises sqlite3.OperationalError ('database or disk is full', 'unable to open database file'), which is not an OSError subclass, so it propagates out of unlock_submit. Additionally backup_to (identilock/db.py:387) writes directly to the final filename — sqlite3.connect creates the file before the copy starts — so a failed backup leaves a zero-byte/partial identilock-auto-*.db behind. That partial file matches the glob 'identilock-*.db', so its fresh mtime suppresses further backup attempts for 7 days, and the name-sorted pruning (automatic[:-AUTO_BACKUP_KEEP]) deletes older good backups while retaining the corrupt newest ones. The manual /settings/backup route (settings_routes.py:273) has no exception handling at all, and move_data_dir/make_move_kit catch only OSError around backup_to with the same gap.
findings.failure_scenario: Disk fills up. User tries to unlock the vault: backup_to raises sqlite3.OperationalError, unlock_submit returns a 500 error page, and the vault cannot be opened at all until space is freed — the exact outcome the code claims to prevent. A truncated identilock-auto-*.db is left in backups/; after the disk recovers, that file's mtime defers the next auto backup a week, and over time pruning discards valid older backups in favor of corrupt ones. When the user later needs a backup after real data loss, the newest 'backups' are unreadable.
findings.fix: In _maybe_auto_backup catch (OSError, sqlite3.Error) — or Exception — as the docstring intends. In db.backup_to, write to a temporary name (e.g. destination.with_suffix('.tmp')) and os.replace() onto the final name only after the backup completes (optionally after PRAGMA integrity_check on the copy), and unlink the temp on failure. Give /settings/backup a try/except (OSError, sqlite3.Error) that renders an error message, and widen the excepts in move_data_dir and make_move_kit the same way.

findings.title: Moved-data pointer scheme can resolve to the wrong directory or strand the vault entirely
findings.description: The only link from the default data dir to a moved vault is a data_dir key in the old folder's prefs.json. Two concrete failure modes: (1) write_prefs merges into existing prefs and move_data_dir (settings_routes.py:141) never clears a stale data_dir key at the destination, so after moving A→B and later back B→A, A's prefs still say data_dir=B while B's say data_dir=A. load_settings' cycle detection (candidate in seen → break) then resolves to B — the opposite of what the UI just told the user ('copied to A and will be used next time'). (2) The success message tells the user 'The old copy stays at <old dir> — delete it yourself'; deleting that folder (the natural reading) also deletes the pointer, so the next launch resolves to the pristine default dir, finds no database, and shows the first-run setup screen. write_prefs is also a non-atomic truncate-and-write, so a crash mid-write corrupts the pointer file with the same stranding effect.
findings.failure_scenario: User moves data from the default folder A to a USB/synced folder B, confirms it works, and deletes folder A as instructed. Next launch: default_data_dir()=A exists but is empty, no pointer, is_initialized is false — the app presents the setup screen as if no vault exists. A non-technical coworker concludes their SSNs/PINs are gone (or worse, runs setup and creates a fresh vault at A, burying the real one at B). In the A→B→A round-trip case, the app silently keeps using the stale copy at B; when the user deletes B as 'the old copy', A's stale pointer still resolves to the now-empty B and the setup screen appears while the live vault sits intact at A.
findings.fix: In move_data_dir, explicitly clear the pointer at the destination: write_prefs(target, lock_minutes=..., data_dir=None) (write_prefs already drops None values). On startup, when the resolved directory actually contains identilock.db, self-heal by rewriting its prefs without a data_dir key. Make write_prefs atomic (write temp file + os.replace). Change the message to name the exact file to delete (identilock.db), warn against deleting the folder itself, and consider having load_settings fall back to scanning the pointer chain for any hop that still contains identilock.db before declaring the vault uninitialized.

findings.title: After 'move my data', the running session keeps writing to the old folder; those edits are silently dropped
findings.description: move_data_dir copies the database to the new folder, writes the pointer, and then leaves app.state.settings pointing at the old directory ('Until then this session keeps using the current folder'). Every write for the rest of the session — new people, freeze PINs, confirmation numbers — goes only to the old copy, which the user is simultaneously told to delete once the new location 'works'. Nothing carries those post-move edits to the new folder. get_conn resolves settings.db_path per request, so switching live is trivial (save_lock_timeout already mutates app.state.settings via dataclasses.replace).
findings.failure_scenario: User moves data to a new folder, then in the same session records the Equifax freeze PIN and confirmation number they just received. They restart Identilock later, see their data at the new location (missing the PIN, which they don't notice), and delete the old folder as instructed. The PIN and confirmation number are permanently gone.
findings.fix: After the copy and pointer write succeed, immediately repoint the app: request.app.state.settings = dataclasses.replace(settings, data_dir=target). Subsequent requests then open the new database. Alternatively, drop all sessions and force a re-unlock so no further writes can hit the old copy; either way, remove the 'until then this session keeps using the current folder' behavior.

findings.title: Decrypt failure returns None, indistinguishable from empty; a subsequent save silently overwrites the ciphertext with NULL
findings.description: Vault.decrypt maps InvalidTag/ValueError to None — the same value as a legitimately empty field. Every read/edit/save round-trip then treats 'unreadable' as 'blank': the person edit form (repo._row_to_person → person_form.html) shows empty email/phone/address/birth_date/notes fields and an unchecked store_full_ssn box (has_full_ssn is False when ssn_enc fails to decrypt), so saving any unrelated edit writes encrypted-None over the original ciphertexts; display_name renders as the literal '(unreadable)' and that string gets saved as the real name. The freeze detail form does the same for PIN/confirmation, and letters._mark_mailed (letters.py:82) writes existing.pin back even when it decrypted to None — no user form involved. The corruption is never surfaced anywhere: a tampered or partially-restored database renders as a normal-looking vault with blanks, so the user never learns they should restore from a backup, and the first save destroys the evidence.
findings.failure_scenario: A user's cloud-sync tool half-restores an old identilock.db (or a disk error corrupts a page): several blobs no longer authenticate. The app shows the person with blank SSN/notes and no warning. The user fixes a typo in the phone number and saves — ssn_enc, notes_enc etc. are overwritten with NULL and the name becomes the string '(unreadable)'. The corrupted-but-diagnostic ciphertext is gone, the user was never told anything was wrong, and the window to restore from a good backup passes unnoticed.
findings.fix: Distinguish the three states: None (no blob), '' or value (decrypted), and a sentinel/flag for 'failed to decrypt'. Surface unreadable fields in the UI ('this field could not be decrypted — restore from a backup') and refuse to overwrite a still-present ciphertext when the in-memory value is the unreadable sentinel (skip that column in UPDATE). At minimum, log/flash a per-page warning whenever any decrypt fails so corruption is loud instead of silent.

findings.title: Recovery wrap is not updated inside the change_passphrase transaction; a crash leaves has_recovery=True with a dead wrap
findings.description: change_passphrase re-keys every field and commits, but the recovery_* meta keys are untouched in that transaction; both call sites (settings_routes.change_passphrase:209, auth.recover_submit:225) call db.set_recovery afterwards as a separate commit, with a multi-second Argon2 derivation in between. If the process dies or set_recovery fails (e.g. disk full) in that window, the stored recovery_wrap still wraps the retired data key. has_recovery() stays True, so the Settings page and the /recover screen both claim a recovery code exists, but recover_data_key will always fail the verifier check — every code, including the one on the user's printed sheet, reports 'did not open the vault'.
findings.failure_scenario: User changes their passphrase; the laptop loses power right after the rewrap transaction commits but before set_recovery completes. Months later they forget the new passphrase and confidently type their saved recovery code: it can never work, the UI gives no hint the code is stale, and the vault (SSNs, freeze PINs for the whole family) is permanently lost even though the user did everything the app told them to.
findings.fix: Fold recovery-wrap maintenance into the same transaction: either generate the new code before BEGIN and write the new recovery_* keys inside change_passphrase's transaction, or at minimum DELETE the recovery_* meta rows inside that transaction so a crash leaves has_recovery honestly False ('no recovery code — issue one from Settings') instead of advertising a dead one.

findings.title: Request in flight during change_passphrase can seal fields under the retired key
findings.description: SessionStore.create() clears all sessions, but it is called only after db.change_passphrase returns — a window of several seconds (Argon2 derivation plus full-table rewrap). A write request that passed dependency resolution before that point holds the old Vault; its UPDATE blocks on change_passphrase's BEGIN IMMEDIATE lock and then applies after the rewrap commits, storing ciphertext sealed with the old key. Under the new key those blobs decrypt to None — silent, permanent loss of exactly-just-saved data (compounded by the decrypt-None finding above).
findings.failure_scenario: User has the app open in both the pywebview window and a browser tab. They submit a person edit in one at nearly the same moment they submit a passphrase change in the other. The edit's UPDATE waits out the rewrap lock, then writes old-key ciphertexts; from then on that person's fields read as blank and the original values are unrecoverable.
findings.fix: Drop all sessions (request.app.state.sessions.drop_all()) before starting db.change_passphrase, so concurrent requests 401 instead of writing; or have change_passphrase bump a key-generation counter checked by Vault.encrypt so a retired vault refuses to seal.

findings.title: setup_import never runs schema migration or seeding on the imported database until the app restarts
findings.description: The upgrade block in web.create_app (create_schema/_ensure_column, seed_agencies, backfill_all_freeze_records, web.py:89-99) runs only at startup, and only if the database is already initialized. setup_import replaces identilock.db afterwards and just redirects to /unlock. A move file produced by an older Identilock release lacks later-added agency columns (action_kind, action_note, protects, impact), and _row_to_agency indexes them unconditionally, so every page that lists agencies raises IndexError.
findings.failure_scenario: Coworker installs the current Identilock on a new machine and imports a move file made by last year's version on the old machine. Unlock succeeds, then the dashboard and every agency-touching page return 500 errors. The data is intact but the app appears broken; it silently heals only after the user thinks to quit and relaunch, which nothing tells them to do.
findings.fix: After scratch.replace(settings.db_path), open a fresh connection and run the same upgrade sequence as create_app (db.create_schema, seed_agencies, backfill_all_freeze_records) before redirecting to /unlock — or factor that block into a shared upgrade_database(conn) helper called from both places.

findings.title: People-list progress counts FYI agencies and ignores not_applicable, so the meter is unreachable and disagrees with the dashboard
findings.description: people_index computes total=len(agencies) over all active agencies including action_kind='fyi' ones, and its done count includes not_applicable records while total does not exclude them. household_progress (repo.py:820) deliberately excludes FYI rows and skips not_applicable records precisely so the meter is honest — the comment says counting them 'would teach people the number is meaningless'. ensure_freeze_records creates rows for FYI agencies too, but the matrix UI offers no way to complete them, so the person-list count can never reach its own denominator and never matches the dashboard's number.
findings.failure_scenario: A household with 7 actionable agencies and 2 FYI entries finishes every freeze. The dashboard says 100% / 7 of 7 done; the People page shows 7/9 for each person forever. A user chasing the missing 2 finds nothing to do; the 'green light' story the numbers tell is inconsistent.
findings.fix: In people_index, filter to [a for a in agencies if not a.is_fyi] and mirror household_progress's per-record logic (skip not_applicable from the denominator) — or better, call household_progress per person so there is exactly one counting rule. Optionally stop creating freeze_records rows for FYI agencies in ensure_freeze_records.

findings.title: User-typed reminder text and report filenames are stored in plaintext, contradicting the 'everything is scrambled' claims
findings.description: The UI repeatedly makes an absolute claim: help.html ('Everything you type is saved into one scrambled (encrypted) file'), settings.html ('a single scrambled database file... unreadable without your passphrase'), the move-kit message ('everything is packaged into one file... scrambled like everything else... useless without the passphrase'), and the move FAQ ('without your passphrase it's gibberish'). But the reminders table stores `title` and `detail` as plain TEXT (db.py lines 135-136), and /reminders accepts free-text user input straight into them (routes/reminders.py reminder_create -> repo.create_reminder, repo.py lines 563-578) with no encryption. Likewise reports.source_name (db.py line 150) stores the uploaded credit-report filename in the clear (routes/reports.py line 99). Even db.py's own 'Left in the clear' docstring (lines 9-14) omits these, claiming a thief 'learns no identities'. The reminders page invites exactly this kind of content ('What' / 'Detail' boxes, person selector) and its own .ics warning admits titles 'include family members' names' — yet nothing tells the user those titles sit unencrypted in the vault file they are told is gibberish without the passphrase.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker adds a custom reminder 'Call Equifax about Emma Arvan's freeze — PIN letter due' and uploads 'Experian_Report_Dan_Arvan.pdf'. They then use 'Package Everything for the Move', and the USB stick is lost — the exact scenario the help page calls safe ('the file is scrambled: without your passphrase it's gibberish'). Anyone opening the .db with any SQLite viewer reads the child's name, the freeze context, and the family surname from reminders.title/detail and reports.source_name in the clear, despite the app's explicit promise that this cannot happen.
findings.fix: Encrypt reminder title/detail (the reminders table already has an unused notes_enc column demonstrating the pattern; add title_enc/detail_enc and migrate, or move user text into notes_enc) and encrypt or drop reports.source_name. Seeded template reminders contain no personal data and could stay queryable if per-row plaintext is desired, but user-entered text must go through vault.encrypt. Also correct db.py's 'Left in the clear' docstring, and until the fix ships, soften the absolute UI claims (help.html, settings.html, move-kit message).

findings.title: Help FAQ claims the breach check sends no personal information, but the email check sends the email address to HIBP
findings.description: help.html's first FAQ answers 'Is my information being sent anywhere?' with: the Breaches page 'asks a public leak-checking service a question when you press Check... Neither sends your personal information anywhere.' That is false for the email check: hibp.check_email (services/hibp.py lines 96-113) transmits the full email address to haveibeenpwned.com — hibp.py's own docstring says so ('This one does send the email address to HIBP'), and breaches.html line 55-59 discloses it honestly ('Fair warning: this one does send the email address'). The 'Check the Whole Family at Once' button sends every family member's stored email. The help page — the page a nervous non-technical user is most likely to trust — flatly contradicts both.
findings.failure_scenario: A privacy-anxious coworker reads the Help FAQ, concludes no personal information ever leaves the machine, and runs 'Check the Whole Family at Once'. Every family member's email address is transmitted to a third-party service — behavior the page they relied on explicitly said does not happen.
findings.fix: Reword the help.html FAQ to match breaches.html: the password check sends only a partial hash; the email check does send the address itself (that is the only way to ask the question), and only when a paid key the user configured is present.

findings.title: The 'What This App Sends Over the Internet' list is presented as complete but omits the Sources link check and HIBP key validation
findings.description: settings.html's summary card states 'Nothing, unless you use the Breaches page'. Two other code paths touch the network: (1) POST /sources/check ('Check All Links Now') fetches all ~31 registry URLs (routes/dashboard.py lines 165-198 -> services/linkcheck.py); (2) saving an HIBP API key POSTs it to HIBP's /subscription/status endpoint before storing (routes/settings_routes.py save_hibp_key line 172 -> hibp.verify_key lines 162-183). The same over-broad exclusivity appears in breaches.html line 8 ('This page is the one part of Identilock that talks to the internet') and setup.html lines 84-86 ('The one thing it can look up on the internet is whether an email or password has shown up in a known leak'). Each feature is disclosed honestly on its own page (sources.html line 44-46, settings key hint line 134), but every global summary that claims completeness is wrong — and this app's core pitch is that its claims are auditable.
findings.failure_scenario: A user (or the coworker who vets the app before giving it out) reads the settings summary and setup page, concludes the Breaches page is the only network path, and runs the app behind a firewall rule permitting only haveibeenpwned.com. 'Check All Links Now' then fails mysteriously — or, worse, they assert to others 'it only ever talks to HIBP' and are provably wrong when someone watches the traffic to equifax.com, irs.gov, etc.
findings.fix: Amend the settings list to enumerate all three paths (breach checks; the Sources page link checker, which fetches the cited agency pages; HIBP key validation on save). Change breaches.html's 'the one part' and setup.html's 'the one thing' to accurate phrasing, mirroring help.html which already lists the link checker.

findings.title: Uploaded credit reports over 1MB are spooled to a plaintext temp file on disk despite the 'never written to disk' claim
findings.description: reports.py comments 'The uploaded file itself is never written to disk — only its extracted text, encrypted, inside the database', and reports.html tells the user 'Identilock keeps only the words from the file, scrambled (encrypted) into its database on this computer.' But the upload arrives via Starlette's multipart parser, which spools any part larger than 1MB (spool_max_size = 1024*1024, starlette/formparsers.py line 147) into a real SpooledTemporaryFile in the OS temp directory. MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES is 25MB, and bureau PDF reports routinely exceed 1MB, so the full plaintext credit report — accounts, SSN, addresses — is written unencrypted to disk during the request. The file is unlinked afterward, but its blocks persist and are recoverable, which matters under the app's own threat model (stolen laptop/disk). The same mechanism applies to /setup/import, though that payload is already an encrypted vault.
findings.failure_scenario: A user uploads a 5MB Experian PDF. Starlette writes all 5MB in the clear to the system temp directory before extract_text runs. The laptop is later stolen; forensic carving of unallocated space on the disk recovers the full credit report even though the vault file itself is unreadable — exactly the disclosure the encrypted-at-rest design promises to prevent, and the code comment claims cannot happen.
findings.fix: Read the request body directly into memory with a size cap instead of going through UploadFile's spooled parser (e.g. stream request body with an in-memory buffer and reject past MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES), or explicitly raise the spool threshold above the max upload size for this route. At minimum, correct the code comment and the reports.html hint so the claim matches behavior.

findings.title: Green light says address 'checked against the agency's own paperwork', but TransUnion's address was only verified against a third-party page
findings.description: agency_detail.html renders, for any agency with address_verified, the green tag '✓ checked against the agency's own paperwork'. For TransUnion (seeds.py lines 193-194, 217-218) the mail_address citation is solely 'ca-ag-child-freeze' — the California Attorney General's page — not any TransUnion document. The CA AG page was genuinely fetched and read, so the sources-page wording ('a person actually read that page on the date shown') is honest, but 'the agency's own paperwork' is literally false for this row. Equifax, Experian, Innovis, LexisNexis, ChexSystems, and NCTUE all cite the organization's own pages, so TransUnion is the one entry where the wording over-claims — on the agency whose packet contains a child's birth certificate and Social Security card.
findings.failure_scenario: TransUnion moves its protected-consumer P.O. box and updates transunion.com; the CA AG page stays stale but alive, so the link checker shows green too. A user sees '✓ checked against the agency's own paperwork', gives the address more trust than it earned, skims past the double-check warnings, and mails a birth certificate and SSN card to the abandoned box.
findings.fix: Make the tag wording follow the citation: 'checked against the agency's own paperwork' only when the fetched source's publisher is the agency itself; otherwise 'confirmed at a government source (California AG), read on DATE'. Alternatively re-verify TransUnion's address against a TransUnion-published document and cite that.

findings.title: Link-checker's 'alive' result reuses the same green verified tag styling as 'read on DATE', inviting conflation
findings.description: In the sources table, the content-verification column renders '✓ read 2026-08-03' with class src-primary (green), and the link-check column renders '✓ alive' with the identical class and checkmark (line 71). The explainer box at the top defines green as 'a person actually opened this page on that date and copied the facts straight out of it' — a meaning the 'alive' tag does not carry (linkcheck.py's docstring is explicit that a working URL 'proves the page exists, not that its contents still say what was recorded'). The distinction survives only in hover tooltips, which the target audience of non-technical users on a giveaway app will rarely see.
findings.failure_scenario: A 'link only — go check' source (e.g. the Experian Freeze Center) shows a yellow tag next to a green '✓ alive'. A user scanning by color — as the page's own legend teaches them to — reads the green check as 'this one is verified' and skips the 'open the page and see for yourself' step the yellow tag was supposed to force.
findings.fix: Give the link-check result its own neutral style (e.g. a grey/blue 'answers' badge, class src-alive) so green + checkmark remains reserved for the human-verified meaning the legend defines; optionally add a third line to the legend explaining the Link column.

verdicts.title: User-entered reminder title and detail are stored in cleartext
verdicts.failure_scenario: A user creates a custom reminder such as 'Thaw Experian for Sarah before closing — PIN 4821'. The laptop or a synced copy of identilock.db is stolen; `strings identilock.db` prints the name and PIN in the clear, despite the backup UI (identilock/routes/settings_routes.py:279-281) promising the file is 'useless without' the passphrase.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code: reminders.title and reminders.detail are plain TEXT (db.py:135-136); repo.create_reminder (identilock/repo.py:572-576) inserts user-typed free text unencrypted; ENCRYPTED_FIELDS['reminders'] lists only notes_enc, which no form or route ever populates. The db.py docstring (line 6) claims 'free-text notes' are encrypted, and the app itself concedes reminder titles 'include family members' names' (identilock/templates/reminders.html:48) — for the calendar export it warns, but for at-rest storage it does not. The reminders form ('What'/'Detail' inputs, reminders.html:69-96) gives no cleartext warning. This is a direct priority-1 confidentiality leak under the stated theft-of-file threat model, so high severity is correct.
verdicts.fix: Add title_enc/detail_enc BLOB columns via _ensure_column, register them in ENCRYPTED_FIELDS, seal in create_reminder/seed_reminders_for and open in list_reminders (the only SQL ordering used is due_date, which stays cleartext), and migrate existing plaintext rows on first unlock. Until then, the reminders form should state these fields are stored unencrypted.

verdicts.title: Uploaded credit-report filename (source_name) stored in cleartext
verdicts.failure_scenario: User uploads 'Equifax report - Sarah Arvan 2026.pdf'. A thief with only the stolen database file reads the filename in the clear and learns a household member's full name and which bureau reports exist for her — the identity linkage the db.py docstring says a stolen file must not reveal ('learns no identities').
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: reports.source_name is plain TEXT (db.py:150), routes/reports.py:99 stores upload.filename verbatim, while text_enc/extracted_enc in the same row are encrypted. Bureau download filenames routinely contain the person's name. The route even comments 'The uploaded file itself is never written to disk' (reports.py:90) while writing its name in cleartext. Medium is right: it leaks identity linkage but not SSNs/PINs, and only when the filename happens to contain a name.
verdicts.fix: Rename to source_name_enc, add it to ENCRYPTED_FIELDS['reports'], seal in save_report and open in _row_to_report (it is display-only — reports.html:80 — so no SQL depends on it); or stop storing the filename and keep only the extension or a generic label. Migrate existing rows on first unlock.

verdicts.title: Data written after a data-dir move is silently lost at next launch
verdicts.failure_scenario: User moves the data dir, then in the same session adds a child with SSN and records freeze PINs, quits. Next launch follows the pointer to the click-time snapshot: the child is absent. The vault opens fine, so 'the new location works'; the user deletes the old folder as the success message instructs, and the records are permanently destroyed.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: move_data_dir calls db.backup_to(conn, new_db) at click time (line 130), writes the pointer (line 142), and never updates request.app.state.settings — web.py:39 confirms get_conn opens app.state.settings.db_path per request, so every subsequent write in the session lands in the OLD database. The next launch opens the stale copy. The success message says the session 'keeps using the current folder' but never warns that later changes will not follow the move, and then tells the user to delete the old folder once confirmed working. Raised to high: this is silent, permanent loss of vault data (durability is audit priority 2), with the UI actively steering the user toward destroying the only surviving copy.
verdicts.fix: After the copy succeeds, swap the live app in the same request: request.app.state.settings = dataclasses.replace(settings, data_dir=target, db_path=target/'identilock.db', ...) so get_conn (web.py:39) routes all subsequent writes to the new folder, and run ensure_data_dir on it so the 0700 chmod applies immediately. At minimum, change the message to say changes made after the move will not follow it.

verdicts.title: Recovery code saved as world-readable plaintext file beside the vault it opens
verdicts.failure_scenario: A coworker clicks 'Save to a file' during setup, never moves it, and the laptop is stolen later. The thief opens Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt from the Desktop, uses 'Forgot your passphrase?' against the stolen data dir, and reads every SSN and PIN. On a shared POSIX machine the 0644 file is also readable by other local users.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: recovery_code_save writes via target.write_text (auth.py:143) with no mode restriction — default umask yields 0644 — to ~/Desktop on the same machine holding identilock.db. Laptop theft is squarely inside the stated threat model (theft of the file), and the recovery flow (auth.py:185-228) accepts the code without the passphrase, so co-location fully defeats the encryption. Partially mitigated: the save is user-initiated, and both the file contents (auth.py:138-140) and the follow-up message explicitly warn to move it and not co-locate it with the data file — but nothing enforces this for the stated non-technical audience. Low severity stands: real defect, but opt-in and warned-about; the chmod fix is trivial and worth taking.
verdicts.fix: Create the file 0600 (os.open with O_CREAT|O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC, mode=0o600, or target.touch(mode=0o600) before write_text). Better: have the 'I have stored my code' acknowledgment ask whether the file has been moved off this machine and offer a one-click delete of the Desktop copy.

verdicts.title: Corrupted ciphertext decrypts to None, indistinguishable from empty, and is destroyed on next save
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code: Vault.decrypt (crypto.py:145-150) maps InvalidTag/ValueError to None, the same value as a NULL blob. The person edit form prefills from decrypted values, so an unreadable field renders blank, and update_person (repo.py:144-171) unconditionally re-encrypts every column from form values, writing NULL over the original ciphertext on any save of that person. The one safeguard that exists — the SSN 'blank means keep' logic at routes/people.py:266-271 — preserves existing.ssn, the DECRYPTED value, which is None for an unreadable blob (and has_full_ssn is False so the store_full_ssn checkbox renders unchecked), so even that field is destroyed. This is a durability defect (audit priority 2) in-scope for the theft/restore threat model: crypto.py:148-149 itself anticipates the partial-restore-under-another-passphrase state, and the docstring's 'integrity nuisance rather than a disclosure' claim is contradicted by silent, permanent loss (priority 3 honesty). Medium, not high: it requires a corrupt or key-mismatched blob to exist first, and destruction needs a subsequent edit of that record.
verdicts.fix: Make decryption failure a distinct state (raise or return a sentinel such as Undecryptable instead of None in Vault.decrypt), render such fields as 'unreadable — wrong passphrase or corrupted data' in templates, and in update paths carry the stored blob through unchanged when the corresponding field is unreadable rather than overwriting it with NULL.

verdicts.title: One undecryptable blob makes passphrase change — and therefore recovery — fail entirely
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code: change_passphrase (db.py:296-327) calls open_sealed on every non-NULL blob across all ENCRYPTED_FIELDS with no per-field error handling; the blanket except rolls back and re-raises. Neither caller catches it — settings_routes.py:207 and auth.py:223 — and the app's only exception handler is for HTTPException (web.py:120), so both routes return an unhandled 500. In /recover this occurs AFTER recover_data_key has already verified the code against the verifier (db.py:382), so a cryptographically correct recovery credential cannot open the vault through the UI if even one blob (e.g. a freeze_records notes_enc) is corrupt. The inconsistency is real: Vault.decrypt deliberately tolerates exactly this state day-to-day, so the vault looks healthy while being un-migratable and un-recoverable. Durability priority 2; medium because it requires a pre-existing corrupt/mismatched blob, but the consequence blocks the designated disaster-recovery path with an unexplained 500.
verdicts.fix: In change_passphrase, catch InvalidTag per field and carry the unreadable blob over unchanged, collecting (table, column, pk) of failures and returning them so routes can report 'passphrase changed; N fields could not be re-encrypted and remain unreadable'. At minimum, catch the exception in /settings/passphrase and /recover and render an actionable error instead of a 500.

verdicts.title: Recovery re-wrap is committed separately from passphrase change, leaving a window where the recovery credential is silently destroyed
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code: change_passphrase commits at db.py:324; set_recovery commits independently at db.py:355; all three call sites sequence them as separate transactions (settings_routes.py:207-209, auth.py:223-225, setup at auth.py:89-93). Between the commits the database holds data and verifier under the new key while recovery_wrap still wraps the old key under the old code — recover_data_key would unwrap the old key, fail the verifier check (db.py:382), and report it as a wrong code. The window is wider than a pure crash race: set_recovery performs a full Argon2id derivation (64 MiB, time_cost 3) between the two commits, roughly a second on the old laptops this app targets, and any set_recovery failure (disk full) 500s the route so the new code is never displayed. Mitigations keep this at medium rather than high: passphrase changes are rare events, and at the moment of failure the user still knows the new passphrase, so loss only materializes if it is later forgotten — but that is exactly the case recovery exists for, the disarming is silent, and the printed Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt explicitly tells the user the code is replaced on passphrase change, so they believe they are covered (priority 3 honesty). The setup-path window (auth.py:89-93) is the mildest case since a crash there just leaves has_recovery false, which /recover reports honestly.
verdicts.fix: Fold the recovery re-wrap into change_passphrase's single transaction: generate the new code and write recovery_salt/recovery_*/recovery_wrap (sealed under the new key) before the single commit at db.py:324, returning (new_vault, code) for the caller to display. Apply the same single-transaction pattern to initial setup.

verdicts.title: No Host-header validation; pre-auth POST endpoints reachable from any website
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code: create_app installs only a security-headers middleware; there is no TrustedHostMiddleware, no Host check, and no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check anywhere in the package. POST /setup (routes/auth.py:68), POST /setup/import (:231), POST /unlock (:290), and POST /recover (:185) require no CSRF token and no session — verify_csrf is only applied to post-unlock routes. The port defaults to a fixed 8731 (config.py:108), so a malicious page can fire blind cross-origin POSTs at it, and DNS rebinding defeats the 'reachable only from this machine' assumption stated in the comment at auth.py:303-304 because nothing rejects a foreign Host. The setup/import hijack window is narrow (only while the vault is uninitialized, is_initialized guards at auth.py:76/242), but the /unlock grinding attack works any time the vault is locked, with no lockout. It is actually slightly worse than claimed: on a successful rebinding-based guess, set_session_cookie issues the session cookie to the attacker's origin, handing the rebinding page an authenticated session to read the vault. This is squarely in-scope under audit priority 4 (CSRF, move-file import). Mitigating factors keeping it medium rather than high: Chrome's Local/Private Network Access restrictions now block or prompt on public-to-loopback requests including rebinding (resolved-IP based), the setup window is brief, and grinding still has to beat Argon2id per guess and a passphrase that passed passphrase_problems.
verdicts.fix: In create_app, add starlette.middleware.trustedhost.TrustedHostMiddleware with allowed_hosts=["localhost", "127.0.0.1", "[::1]"] (append settings.host when IDENTILOCK_ALLOW_REMOTE=1 and the host is non-loopback). Additionally reject the pre-auth POSTs in routes/auth.py when an Origin header is present and does not match the request's own scheme://host, or when Sec-Fetch-Site is present and not 'same-origin'/'none' — same-origin form posts and non-browser clients still pass.

verdicts.title: Settings' "What This App Sends Over the Internet" list is incomplete
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: settings.html:171-172 states 'Nothing, unless you use the Breaches page' and enumerates only the two HIBP lookups, while POST /sources/check (routes/dashboard.py:165-177) fetches all 32 registry URLs via linkcheck.check_links — an egress path the list flatly contradicts. However, half the finding is already mitigated: the HIBP key verification (settings_routes.py:172 -> hibp.verify_key) IS disclosed on this same page — the API-key form's hint at settings.html:134 says 'The key is validated against HIBP before it is saved', so a reader of the Settings page is told about that transmission, just not inside the summary list. The confirmed gap is the Sources link check, which the reviewer notes help.html does mention. No personal data is involved in either path, so this is an honesty-of-claims gap (audit priority 3) at low severity.
verdicts.fix: Add a bullet to the list in settings.html: the Sources page's 'Check All Links Now' makes ordinary page requests to the agency sites listed on Sources (nothing about you is sent), and optionally fold the existing key-validation hint into the list as a second bullet so the summary is self-contained.

verdicts.title: Link-check User-Agent announces Identilock to every agency site, contradicting UI claim
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: USER_AGENT = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Identilock link check)" at linkcheck.py:20 is sent on every probe to all 32 registry URLs (client created with that header at :45). The module's own docstring (:10-11) claims the requests are 'the same anonymous page fetches a browser would make', which the product-naming UA contradicts, and settings.html:178-181 promises agency sites 'do not learn you came from a tool like this' (strictly about referrer suppression on outbound link clicks, but the broader promise the user takes away). The UA does tell every fetched site and on-path middlebox that this IP runs an identity-protection vault — metadata the app elsewhere works to withhold. No personal data is sent, and the check only runs on explicit user action behind CSRF, so this stays low as an honesty/metadata gap rather than a leak.
verdicts.fix: Replace USER_AGENT in linkcheck.py with a generic current-browser UA carrying no product token, and adjust the docstring; or keep the identifying UA (polite-crawler convention) and instead correct the docstring and settings.html so no page claims the fetches are anonymous.

verdicts.title: CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' scripts, neutralizing its XSS backstop on SSN-bearing pages
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: the CSP at web.py:113-116 includes script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline', which permits injected inline script and inline event handlers, so the CSP provides no XSS backstop on pages rendering SSNs, freeze PINs, and uploaded report text. I confirmed the reviewer's supporting claims: no |safe filter is applied to user data anywhere in templates, so Jinja autoescaping is the sole defense today, and the failure scenario is future-conditional (a template regression), which is why this stays a low hardening gap rather than an active defect. One correction to the analysis: the app contains zero <script> elements and zero JS files (static/ holds only app.css) — all JavaScript is inline event handler attributes (onclick/onsubmit in base.html:16-17, letter_print.html:11, person_form.html:160, report_detail.html:85, reminders.html:23, etc.). That means the proposed nonce fallback would not work: CSP nonces do not apply to event-handler attributes. The handlers would need to move to an external file, making the fix a small refactor rather than a header tweak.
verdicts.fix: Create identilock/static/app.js that attaches the handful of behaviors (history back/forward, window.print, delete-confirm via data-confirm attributes) with addEventListener, replace the inline onclick/onsubmit attributes with data attributes, include the script via <script src="/static/app.js"> in base.html, and drop 'unsafe-inline' from script-src. Note that a nonce-based approach alone will not work here because the inline code is entirely event-handler attributes, which nonces do not cover.

findings.title: Uploaded credit reports over 1MB are written to a cleartext OS temp file, contradicting the code's own claim
findings.description: Starlette's MultiPartParser (formparsers.py, spool_max_size = 1024*1024) spools any uploaded file part larger than 1MB into a SpooledTemporaryFile that rolls over to a real file in the system temp directory, in cleartext, before the handler ever runs. Credit report PDFs routinely exceed 1MB and contain full SSNs, DOBs, addresses, and account numbers. The comment at routes/reports.py:90-91 states 'The uploaded file itself is never written to disk — only its extracted text, encrypted, inside the database', which is false for any report over 1MB. The temp file is unlinked after the request, but the plaintext blocks remain recoverable on disk, and the file can persist if the process is killed mid-request — directly inside the stated threat model (protect against theft of what is on disk). The same spooling applies to /setup/import, though that payload is already encrypted.
findings.failure_scenario: User uploads a 4MB Equifax PDF on /reports. Starlette spools it to e.g. /tmp/tmpXXXX (or %TEMP% on the Windows machines coworkers will use) in cleartext, then deletes it. The laptop is later stolen; the vault file is unreadable ciphertext as designed, but the deleted temp file containing the full report — SSN included — is recoverable with trivial undelete tooling, defeating the encryption the app promises.
findings.fix: In create_app (or module import in web.py), raise the spool threshold above the upload cap so parts stay in RAM: `from starlette.formparsers import MultiPartParser; MultiPartParser.spool_max_size = MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (verify the attribute is honored in the installed Starlette version; otherwise read the body via request.stream() and parse the multipart manually). Also correct or qualify the comment and any matching UI copy until the fix is in place.

findings.title: Catastrophic quadratic regex in HTML upload stripping hangs the server indefinitely
findings.description: extract_text strips scripts with re.sub(r"<(script|style)[^>]*>.*?</\1>", ...) using re.S. When the file contains many opening tags with no matching closer, each match attempt lazily scans to end-of-input and fails, giving O(n*m) behavior. Empirically verified in this repo's venv: a 1.6MB input of repeated '<script>' did not complete within 120 seconds (process had to be killed); the 25MB upload cap allows inputs vastly worse. The parse runs synchronously in a FastAPI threadpool worker with no timeout, so the request never returns and the thread is lost until app restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A user is emailed a fake 'credit report.html' (or saves a malformed bureau page) containing thousands of unclosed <script> tags and uploads it on /reports. The request hangs forever, the Save button never responds, and after retrying a few times all threadpool workers are pinned at 100% CPU — the entire app, including /lock, stops responding until the process is killed.
findings.fix: Make the close-tag optional so every match succeeds in one pass (linear): r"<(script|style)[^>]*>.*?(?:</\1\s*>|\Z)" — an unclosed script then swallows the remainder, which is acceptable for text extraction — or replace the regex stripping with html.parser-based extraction. Consider a much smaller size cap for non-PDF uploads; real report text is a few hundred KB as the code itself notes.

findings.title: pypdf text extraction is unbounded: compression-bomb PDFs can exhaust memory despite the 25MB cap
findings.description: MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES limits the input file, but _extract_pdf joins page.extract_text() over every page with no page-count, output-size, or time budget. FlateDecode streams compress ~1000:1, so a small crafted PDF can expand to gigabytes of extracted text; pathological object graphs can also make pypdf extremely slow. The full extracted text is then regex-scanned, encrypted, and inserted into the SQLite vault, permanently bloating the database file even if extraction succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: A crafted 2MB PDF whose content streams decompress to several GB is uploaded; extract_text allocates until the Python process is OOM-killed mid-request, taking the vault app down. In a milder case a 200MB-of-text PDF is stored encrypted into identilock.db, making every subsequent backup and report_detail page load enormous.
findings.fix: Cap extraction: refuse PDFs with more than e.g. 500 pages, truncate per-page and total extracted text (e.g. 5MB total, with a visible 'report text truncated' notice), and check the running total inside the page loop so a bomb stops early instead of after joining.

findings.title: /setup/import has no CSRF or origin check and no size cap, letting a web page plant a vault before first setup
findings.description: setup_import is the only state-changing endpoint with no CSRF token (understandably, since no session exists pre-setup), but it also performs no Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check and no size limit. The app listens on a predictable default (127.0.0.1:8731). Cross-origin top-level form POSTs to loopback are not blocked by browsers, so any website open in the user's browser can submit a multipart body to it. The uploaded bytes are also written to disk (scratch file) with no cap, unlike /reports which enforces 25MB.
findings.failure_scenario: A coworker installs the giveaway app and browses the web before completing setup. A malicious page auto-submits a hidden form to http://127.0.0.1:8731/setup/import containing a valid Identilock database initialized with the attacker's passphrase. The user now sees the unlock screen instead of setup; at best they are confused into wiping data, at worst they follow attacker instructions ('your setup passphrase is X') and type family SSNs into a vault whose passphrase the attacker knows. Separately, a multi-GB POST fills the disk via the uncapped scratch write.
findings.fix: Reject the request unless the Origin header is absent or matches the app's own host (or Sec-Fetch-Site is 'same-origin'/'none'); apply this check to all pre-session POSTs (/setup, /setup/import, /unlock, /recover) for defense in depth. Enforce a size cap on the import body before writing the scratch file.

findings.title: str.isdigit()/int() mismatch and unbounded integers turn junk IDs into 500s instead of clean rejections
findings.description: Three handlers use `value.isdigit()` as a guard before `int(value)`: breaches.py:76 (person_id), letters.py:42 (_pick_guardian), reminders.py:67 (person_id). isdigit() returns True for Unicode digit characters such as superscripts ('²'.isdigit() is True) that int() rejects with ValueError — verified in this repo's venv — producing an unhandled 500. Separately, a plain-ASCII huge value like person_id='9'*25 passes both isdigit() and int(), then raises sqlite3.OverflowError ('Python int too large to convert to SQLite INTEGER') at bind time — also verified; the same applies to path parameters, e.g. GET /people/99999999999999999999999999 returns 500 instead of 404. In breaches_check_email the crash happens after the HIBP API call succeeded, so the lookup result is silently lost.
findings.failure_scenario: POST /breaches/email with person_id='²' (or a 25-digit person_id) while unlocked: the HIBP lookup runs, then save_breach_check raises ValueError/OverflowError, the user gets a bare 500 error page, and the check they paid an API call for is not recorded. GET /letters/all?guardian=² 500s the bulk-print page.
findings.fix: Replace the isdigit() pattern with a helper that does try/except int() and range-checks the result (e.g. 0 < id < 2**63), returning None on failure; for path parameters, add the same bound via Path(..., lt=2**63) or catch OverflowError centrally and return 404.

findings.title: freeze_save does not verify the person/agency exist, so a stale or forged ID yields a 500 via FOREIGN KEY IntegrityError
findings.description: POST /freeze/{person_id}/{agency_id} calls update_freeze_record, whose first step ensure_freeze_records (repo.py:374) INSERTs placeholder rows for the given person_id. Foreign keys are ON (db.py:189), so a nonexistent person_id raises sqlite3.IntegrityError, which no handler catches — the user gets a 500. The GET counterpart (freeze_detail) and the letters routes both check existence first; only the save path skips it.
findings.failure_scenario: User opens a freeze detail form in one tab, deletes that family member in another tab, then submits the form: instead of a 404 or a friendly 'this person was removed' message, the app throws an unhandled IntegrityError 500.
