findings.fix: Mirror letter_mark_mailed: at the top of freeze_save, `if get_person(conn, vault, person_id) is None or get_agency(conn, agency_id) is None: raise HTTPException(404, ...)`.

verdicts.title: Auto-backup catches only OSError; sqlite3 errors block unlock, and failed backups poison the backup set
verdicts.failure_scenario: Disk fills. On unlock, db.backup_to raises sqlite3.OperationalError, which escapes the `except OSError` at auth.py:48 and turns unlock_submit into a 500 — the exact failure the docstring promises to swallow. sqlite3.connect creates the destination file before the copy, so a partial identilock-auto-*.db is left behind; its fresh mtime matches the identilock-*.db glob and suppresses further auto-backups for 7 days (this also means the second unlock attempt usually succeeds — the blocking is typically one attempt, not indefinite — but the corrupt file persists). Name-sorted pruning (automatic[:-10]) then discards older good backups while retaining the corrupt newest ones, so when a backup is actually needed the newest copies are unreadable. The manual /settings/backup route (settings_routes.py:273) has no exception handling at all, and move_data_dir/make_move_kit catch only OSError around backup_to.
verdicts.reasoning: Every element checks out in code. sqlite3.OperationalError inherits sqlite3.Error -> Exception, not OSError, so the except clause at auth.py:48 does not cover it. db.backup_to (db.py:387-396) opens sqlite3.connect(destination) directly at the final name with no temp-file/os.replace step, so the file exists before the copy completes. The glob at auth.py:38 is 'identilock-*.db', matching both manual and auto backups including a truncated one, and the pruning at auth.py:45-46 sorts by name (timestamp-embedded, so chronological) keeping the newest 10 regardless of validity. settings_routes.py:273 calls db.backup_to bare. The only overstatement in the claim is 'cannot be opened at all until space is freed' — in the common sub-case the partial file's mtime makes the retry skip the backup and unlock succeeds; only if file creation itself fails does every unlock 500. The backup-set poisoning is the durable harm and squarely hits audit priority 2 (durability), justifying high.
verdicts.fix: In _maybe_auto_backup catch (OSError, sqlite3.Error) as the docstring intends. In db.backup_to, back up to destination.with_suffix('.tmp') and os.replace() onto the final name only after conn.backup completes, unlinking the temp on failure (optionally run PRAGMA integrity_check on the copy first). Wrap /settings/backup in try/except (OSError, sqlite3.Error) rendering an error message, and widen the excepts around backup_to in move_data_dir and make_move_kit the same way.

verdicts.title: Moved-data pointer scheme can resolve to the wrong directory or strand the vault entirely
verdicts.failure_scenario: (1) Stranding: after 'move my data' the success message says 'The old copy stays at <old dir> — delete it yourself'. A user who deletes that folder also deletes prefs.json — the only pointer to the new location. Next launch, default_data_dir() has no pointer and no database, so is_initialized is false and the app shows the first-run setup screen; a non-technical coworker concludes their SSNs/PINs are gone, or runs setup and creates a fresh empty vault shadowing the real one. (2) Wrong resolution: move A->B, later delete only B's... rather A's identilock.db (as the 'move that file out of the way' error instructs) and move B->A. write_prefs merges, so A's prefs retain the stale data_dir=B alongside the fresh copy; load_settings follows A->B, then B's data_dir=A hits the `candidate in seen` break, and the app silently keeps running from B — the copy the user was just told is old and deletable. (3) write_prefs is a non-atomic truncate-and-write; a crash mid-write corrupts the pointer with the same stranding effect.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified by tracing the code. write_prefs (config.py:36-45) reads existing prefs and prefs.update(updates) — it never removes keys unless explicitly set to None, and move_data_dir (settings_routes.py:141-142) writes only lock_minutes to the target, so a stale data_dir at the destination survives. The round-trip is reachable: move_data_dir refuses a target containing identilock.db and tells the user to 'move that file out of the way first', which removes the db but not prefs.json. load_settings' loop (config.py:97-105) with seen={A}: A->B (B added to seen), B's prefs say A, A in seen -> break, resolved_dir=B. The deletion scenario follows the app's own instruction verbatim ('The old copy stays at {data_dir} — delete it yourself'), and after deletion resolution lands on an empty default dir -> setup screen. write_prefs uses Path.write_text directly, non-atomic. No data is cryptographically destroyed — the vault file survives intact at the other location — but for the stated audience (non-technical coworkers) the practical outcome is a believed-lost vault or a shadow vault splitting new data, which is a durability failure the app itself induces. High is appropriate.
verdicts.fix: In move_data_dir, clear any stale pointer at the destination: write_prefs(target, lock_minutes=..., data_dir=None) (write_prefs already drops None values). At startup, when the resolved directory contains identilock.db, self-heal by rewriting its prefs without a data_dir key. Make write_prefs atomic (write to a temp file, then os.replace). Reword the success message to name the exact file to delete (identilock.db) and warn against deleting the folder; optionally have load_settings fall back to any pointer-chain hop that still contains identilock.db before declaring the vault uninitialized.

verdicts.title: After 'move my data', the running session keeps writing to the old folder; those edits are silently dropped
verdicts.failure_scenario: User moves data to a new folder, then in the same session records a freeze PIN and confirmation number. get_conn (web.py:39) still resolves app.state.settings.db_path to the old directory, so those writes land only in the old copy. After a restart the app uses the new location — missing the PIN, which nothing flags — and the user deletes the old folder as instructed. The PIN and confirmation number are permanently gone.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed directly from the code: move_data_dir copies via backup_to, writes both prefs files, and returns a flash message — it never touches request.app.state.settings, and the message itself admits 'Until then this session keeps using the current folder.' get_conn opens request.app.state.settings.db_path per request, so every subsequent write in the session hits the old copy, and nothing ever reconciles the two databases. The fix is demonstrably cheap: save_lock_timeout in the same file already mutates app.state.settings via dataclasses.replace, and get_conn's per-request resolution means the switch takes effect immediately. Silent permanent loss of just-entered data, but requires the user to keep editing after the move and before restart; medium fits.
verdicts.fix: After the copy and pointer writes succeed, repoint the running app: request.app.state.settings = dataclasses.replace(settings, data_dir=target), so subsequent requests open the new database (get_conn already resolves per request). Alternatively drop all sessions to force re-unlock so no further writes can reach the old copy. Update the flash message accordingly.

verdicts.title: Decrypt failure returns None, indistinguishable from empty; a subsequent save silently overwrites the ciphertext with NULL
verdicts.failure_scenario: A cloud-sync tool half-restores an old identilock.db or a disk error corrupts pages: several blobs fail AES-GCM authentication. Vault.decrypt returns None for each — identical to a legitimately blank field — so the person renders with empty SSN/notes/DOB, has_full_ssn False, and display_name as the literal '(unreadable)' (repo.py:79), with no warning anywhere. The user fixes an unrelated typo and saves: update_person (repo.py:139-171) re-encrypts every field from the round-tripped form, writing NULL over the surviving ciphertexts and '(unreadable)' as the person's real name. letters._mark_mailed (letters.py:82) does the same to pin_enc/confirmation_enc with no user form involved. The diagnostic ciphertext is destroyed, and the window to restore from a good backup passes with the user never told anything was wrong.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed at every step. crypto.py:142-150: InvalidTag/ValueError -> None, conflated with the None returned for an absent blob. repo.py:71-81 builds the Person from those Nones and substitutes '(unreadable)' for the name — a string the edit form then submits as data. update_person unconditionally re-encrypts all eight fields from form values, and Vault.encrypt maps None/'' to NULL, so a save after a decrypt failure replaces still-present ciphertext with NULL. _mark_mailed passes existing.pin/confirmation/notes back through update_freeze_record, so even a click on 'mark mailed' with no form nulls a failed-to-decrypt PIN. No code path logs, flashes, or distinguishes the failure. The trigger requires file corruption or partial restore — not everyday — but the app's whole purpose is surviving exactly that via backups, and this behavior destroys the evidence and the restore window silently. Medium under durability priority is right.
verdicts.fix: Introduce a sentinel for 'ciphertext present but failed to decrypt' distinct from None. In _row_to_person/_row_to_freeze, carry that sentinel; in update paths, skip columns whose in-memory value is the sentinel so surviving ciphertext is never overwritten; stop saving the '(unreadable)' placeholder as data. Surface a visible per-page warning whenever any field fails to decrypt ('this field could not be read — restore from a backup').

verdicts.title: Recovery wrap is not updated inside the change_passphrase transaction; a crash leaves has_recovery=True with a dead wrap
verdicts.failure_scenario: User changes their passphrase; the laptop dies right after change_passphrase's transaction commits but before the separate set_recovery commit — a window widened to seconds by set_recovery's Argon2 derivation (KdfParams.generate + derive_key at db.py:348-349). The stored recovery_wrap still wraps the retired data key while has_recovery() reports True. Months later the user forgets the passphrase and enters their printed recovery code: recover_data_key unwraps the old data key but check_verifier against the new verifier fails, so every code — including the correct saved one — reports 'did not open the vault'. The UI gives no hint the code is stale; the vault is permanently lost despite the user doing everything right.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed in db.py: change_passphrase (283-329) rewraps fields and meta and commits, touching no recovery_* keys. Both call sites (settings_routes.py:207-209, auth.py:223-225) invoke db.set_recovery afterward as an independent commit, and set_recovery performs a fresh Argon2id derivation before writing — a multi-hundred-ms-to-seconds crash window on the five-year-old laptops the code itself anticipates. In the crash state: has_recovery() true (recovery_wrap present), recover_data_key succeeds in opening the wrap with the old code but returns None at the verifier check (db.py:382-383), and the /recover UI (auth.py:211) reports a wrong code. The failure needs a crash in a narrow window plus a later forgotten passphrase, but the consequence is total, silent, permanent vault loss with the safety net actively lying about its existence. Medium is the right weight.
verdicts.fix: Move recovery maintenance into change_passphrase's transaction: generate the new code and recovery params before BEGIN and write the recovery_* meta rows inside the same transaction that swaps the verifier; or, at minimum, DELETE the recovery_* rows inside that transaction so a crash leaves has_recovery honestly False and the UI directs the user to reissue a code from Settings.

verdicts.title: Request in flight during change_passphrase can seal fields under the retired key
verdicts.failure_scenario: The app is open in the pywebview window and a browser tab (both explicitly supported). The user submits a person edit in one at nearly the same moment as a passphrase change in the other. The edit passed get_vault before sessions were cleared, so it holds the old Vault and seals with the old key; its UPDATE blocks on change_passphrase's BEGIN IMMEDIATE lock (sqlite's default 5 s busy timeout comfortably outlasts the rewrap of this tiny database — the Argon2 derivation happens before BEGIN) and commits after the rewrap. Those blobs then decrypt to None under the new key: the just-saved fields read as blank forever, compounded by the silent decrypt-None overwrite behavior.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed: SessionStore.create (security.py:53-62) clears sessions, but settings_routes.py:207-208 calls it only after db.change_passphrase returns, so any request that resolved its dependencies earlier retains the old Vault for its whole handler. db.change_passphrase derives the new key before BEGIN IMMEDIATE (db.py:294-297), so the write lock is held only for the small rewrap loop, well inside the concurrent connection's default 5-second busy timeout — the blocked UPDATE proceeds after commit rather than erroring. This is a race between two windows of the same legitimate user, not the out-of-scope malware threat, so it is in scope. Requires near-simultaneous submissions in a single-user app: genuinely narrow, hence low.
verdicts.fix: Call request.app.state.sessions.drop_all() before db.change_passphrase so concurrent requests get 401/redirect instead of writing with the retired vault (auth.recover_submit needs the same treatment); or add a key-generation counter that Vault.encrypt checks so a retired vault refuses to seal.

verdicts.title: setup_import never runs schema migration or seeding on the imported database until the app restarts
verdicts.failure_scenario: Coworker installs current Identilock on a new machine and imports a move file made by an older release lacking the later-added agency columns (action_kind, action_note, protects, impact). setup_import validates only is_initialized, replaces identilock.db, and redirects to /unlock. Unlock succeeds, then the dashboard and every agency-listing page 500: list_agencies does SELECT *, and _row_to_agency (repo.py:280-283) indexes row['action_kind'] etc. unconditionally — sqlite3.Row raises IndexError for a missing column. The upgrade block in create_app (web.py:89-99) runs only at process start, so the app appears broken until the user happens to quit and relaunch, which nothing suggests.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed from the code: auth.py:274-276 closes the connection, replaces the file, and redirects with no create_schema/_ensure_column/seed_agencies call; the only migration path is create_app's startup block, which has already run (and skipped work, since the db was uninitialized then). _ensure_column's existence (db.py:220-229) proves databases without these columns are an anticipated, supported input, and _row_to_agency reads all four bolted-on columns unconditionally. The failure is a temporary 500-everywhere state with zero data loss, self-healing on restart — exactly a low-severity usability/durability-of-experience defect, though nasty for the non-technical audience.
verdicts.fix: After scratch.replace(settings.db_path), open a fresh connection and run the same upgrade sequence as create_app — db.create_schema(conn), seed_agencies(conn), backfill_all_freeze_records(conn) — before redirecting to /unlock; ideally factor that block into a shared upgrade_database(conn) helper called from both places.

verdicts.title: People-list progress counts FYI agencies and ignores not_applicable, so the meter is unreachable and disagrees with the dashboard
verdicts.failure_scenario: A household finishes every actionable freeze. The dashboard (household_progress) says 7 of 7 done; the People page says 7/9 per person forever, because its total=len(agencies) includes the two seeded action_kind='fyi' agencies (seeds.py has two such entries) whose freeze_records rows exist (ensure_freeze_records inserts for every active agency) but which the matrix UI deliberately never offers status controls for (freezes.py:40-43 lists them below the grid). A not_applicable record also counts as done in people.py (is_done includes it) while household_progress removes it from the denominator, so the two meters disagree in a second way. A user chasing the missing entries finds nothing to do.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed: people.py:80-85 computes done over cells where is_done (which includes 'not_applicable', repo.py:340) against total=len(agencies) with no is_fyi or not_applicable filtering; household_progress (repo.py:820-841) filters both, and its own comment explains why counting FYI rows makes the meter meaningless. ensure_freeze_records (repo.py:374-390) creates rows for all is_active agencies including FYI, and matrix_view excludes FYI agencies from the actionable grid, so those records can never leave not_started through the UI — the people-list denominator is genuinely unreachable. This is a consistency/honesty-of-progress-numbers defect (audit priority 3/5 territory) with no data at risk: low is correct.
verdicts.fix: In people_index, mirror household_progress: filter agencies to non-FYI and skip not_applicable records from the denominator — or simply call household_progress per person so a single counting rule exists. Optionally stop creating freeze_records rows for FYI agencies in ensure_freeze_records.

verdicts.title: /setup and /setup/import accept cross-origin POSTs, letting a web page set the vault passphrase on a fresh install
verdicts.reasoning: Verified in code. POST /setup (auth.py:68), POST /setup/import (auth.py:231) and POST /recover (auth.py:185) take no csrf_token parameter and never call verify_csrf; the corresponding templates (setup.html, recover.html, unlock.html) contain no csrf field at all (grep for 'csrf' in them returns nothing). A repo-wide grep for Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch/TrustedHost in identilock/ returns nothing, and web.py:101-118 installs only a response-header middleware, so no request-side origin check exists. Both endpoints are reachable with no cookie (no get_session/require_session dependency), so SameSite=strict is irrelevant to reaching them, and the app's own CSP form-action 'self' constrains the app's pages, not the attacker's. A cross-origin auto-submitting form therefore does call db.initialize_vault(conn, passphrase) with an attacker-chosen passphrase, or replaces the fresh DB via /setup/import. Two corrections that lower the severity from the reviewer's 'high': (a) both endpoints are hard-gated by 'if db.is_initialized(conn): return redirect(...)', so the entire window is the minutes between install and first passphrase — after that the gap is unexploitable, and /recover additionally needs a valid recovery code, so it is not attackable at all; (b) the 'victim finds it already unlocked' step needs the Set-Cookie to actually stick, which only holds for a top-level form navigation (visible to the user, and useless if they run the default pywebview window, which has its own cookie jar) — in a hidden iframe modern third-party-cookie blocking drops it, leaving only lockout/DoS on an empty vault. The defect is real and the fix is cheap, but the reachable worst case is narrower than described.
verdicts.fix: Issue a random pre-session cookie plus a matching hidden token on GET /setup and GET /recover and verify it on the matching POSTs, and/or add one middleware in create_app that rejects any non-GET/HEAD request whose Origin is present and not the app's own origin, or whose Sec-Fetch-Site is neither same-origin nor none. The middleware closes this class for every current and future endpoint at once.

verdicts.title: Uploaded credit reports are written to an unencrypted OS temp file, contradicting the in-app claim
verdicts.reasoning: Every technical claim checks out against the installed Starlette. formparsers.py:147 sets MultiPartParser.spool_max_size = 1024*1024 and line 230 backs each file part with SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=self.spool_max_size), so any upload past 1 MB rolls over to a real tempfile.TemporaryFile in the OS temp directory. formparsers.py:184 applies max_part_size only when _current_part.file is None, so file parts are indeed unbounded. reports.py:70 does 'data = await upload.read()' and the MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES check is at line 73 — after parsing, so it cannot prevent the spill. Meanwhile reports.py:90-91 states 'The uploaded file itself is never written to disk' and templates/reports.html tells the user Identilock 'keeps only the words from the file, scrambled (encrypted) into its database on this computer'. Both are false for the common case of a multi-MB bureau PDF containing the full SSN. This lands squarely on audit priority 1, which names temp files explicitly, and on priority 3 (honesty). Platform nuance worth noting but not disqualifying: on Linux tempfile.TemporaryFile uses O_TMPFILE so no other process can open it by path; on Windows — the stated coworker platform — it is a named %TEMP% file, and on all platforms the plaintext blocks remain unwiped after close on a machine without full-disk encryption. Keeping the reviewer's 'high': plaintext SSN-bearing data reaches the disk in the clear and the app states the opposite.
verdicts.fix: Reject POST /reports before parsing when Content-Length exceeds MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (middleware or dependency), then raise starlette.formparsers.MultiPartParser.spool_max_size above that cap at startup so the body never rolls to disk. Fix the comment at reports.py:90-91 and the hint in templates/reports.html to match whatever the code actually does.

verdicts.title: No Host-header validation, so a remote site can reach the loopback app via DNS rebinding
verdicts.reasoning: Accurate as to the code: create_app mounts only the security_headers middleware, no TrustedHostMiddleware and no Host check anywhere (grep for TrustedHost across identilock/ is empty), and uvicorn is started in cli.py:111 with no host filtering, so the app answers any Host. DNS rebinding to 127.0.0.1:8731 is therefore mechanically possible. I am downgrading medium to low because the impact is almost entirely derivative of finding 1 and each of the reviewer's payloads is weaker than stated: the session cookie is host-scoped, so no existing session can be ridden; every route that returns decrypted data (/people, /matrix, /freeze/{p}/{a}, /reports) depends on get_vault/get_session and 401s to /unlock without a session, so the only lever is POST /setup, which again requires an uninitialized vault — the same narrow window, now behind the much higher bar of controlling a domain, pinning the same port, and holding the victim's tab open across the rebind. The remaining POST /unlock oracle is bounded by Argon2id and yields nothing against a passphrase that is not already guessable. Real gap, standard hardening, but low expected impact here.
verdicts.fix: app.add_middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=["127.0.0.1", "localhost", "::1"]) in create_app, built from settings.host, before the routers are included.

verdicts.title: Move file and recovery code are both dropped on ~/Desktop with default permissions — the app violates its own warning
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed on all the parts that live in the code. settings_routes.py:238-243 targets Path.home()/'Desktop' and writes the full vault via db.backup_to; auth.py:127-143 writes the plaintext recovery code to Path.home()/'Desktop'/'Identilock-Recovery-Code.txt' — the same directory. The code is genuinely a second key: db.recover_data_key (db.py:363-384) derives a recovery key and unwraps the data key directly, no passphrase involved, so the two files together are the plaintext vault. The contradiction is in the app's own text: auth.py:139-140 tells the user 'not in the same place as a copy of the data file itself' while the app defaults both to one folder. Permissions confirmed too: db.backup_to (db.py:387-396) uses plain sqlite3.connect on the destination and Path.write_text uses the default umask, so both land 0644 on POSIX, while config.ensure_data_dir deliberately chmods the data dir and backup dir to 0700 — the app protects the copies it keeps and not the copies it hands the user. The cloud-sync half (iCloud Desktop sync, OneDrive Known Folder Move) is environmental and I could not verify it from the repo, but it does not carry the finding: the same-directory placement plus 0644 is sufficient on its own. Medium is right; it needs deliberate user clicks on both features.
verdicts.fix: Create both files with mode 0600 (os.open with 0o600, or write then os.chmod). Default the move file to settings.data_dir rather than the Desktop and show the resulting path, keep the recovery code in a different directory, and state on screen that the Desktop is cloud-synced on most machines so the choice is deliberate.

verdicts.title: /setup/import buffers and writes an upload of unbounded size
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: auth.py:246 does 'data = await upload.read()' with no size check whatsoever — unlike /reports there is not even the post-hoc MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES test — and line 251 then does scratch.write_bytes(data) into the data directory. The claim that Starlette's max_part_size does not bound file parts is correct (formparsers.py:184 checks it only when the part has no file), so the body is limited only by RAM and disk. The cleanup gap is also real: scratch is removed only on the validation-failure branch (line 261) or implicitly by scratch.replace on success, so an OSError/MemoryError between write_bytes and either exit leaves identilock.import-tmp behind with no cleanup path. Low is correct: the endpoint is gated on an uninitialized vault, the worst outcome is a crashed process, a filled disk, and a stray junk file next to an empty database — no data loss and no disclosure — and the leftover name does not collide with identilock.db.
verdicts.fix: Reject the request when Content-Length exceeds a few-MB cap, stream the upload to the scratch path in chunks with a running counter and abort past the cap, and wrap the whole scratch lifecycle in try/finally so no partial import file is ever left in the data directory.

verdicts.title: User-typed reminder text and report filenames are stored in plaintext, contradicting the 'everything is scrambled' claims
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced in code: db.py declares reminders.title/detail as plain TEXT (lines 135-136) and ENCRYPTED_FIELDS lists only notes_enc for reminders (line 50); repo.create_reminder inserts the user's title/detail directly into those columns with no vault involvement, and routes/reminders.py reminder_create passes free-text form input straight through. reports.source_name (db.py:150) likewise stores the uploaded filename in the clear via save_report (repo.py:635-641, routes/reports.py:99). The contradicted absolute claims are verbatim in help.html:16 ('Everything you type is saved into one scrambled (encrypted) file'), help.html:78 (lost USB is 'gibberish'), settings.html:15-17 ('unreadable without your passphrase'), and the move-kit success message (settings_routes.py:251-256, 'useless without the passphrase'). db.py's own 'Left in the clear' docstring (lines 9-14) omits these fields and claims a thief 'learns no identities' — false once a reminder names a family member or a report filename contains one. This is both a priority-1 confidentiality defect (names/context readable in the stolen file, the exact threat the app defends against) and a priority-3 honesty defect, so high severity holds.
verdicts.fix: Encrypt user-entered reminder text (add title_enc/detail_enc BLOBs following the existing notes_enc pattern, migrate existing rows via _ensure_column plus a backfill under the vault key, and add them to ENCRYPTED_FIELDS so passphrase changes re-wrap them) and encrypt or stop storing reports.source_name. Seeded template reminders contain no personal data and may stay plaintext if needed for SQL sorting, but anything from the /reminders form must go through vault encryption. Correct the db.py 'Left in the clear' docstring; until the schema fix ships, soften the absolute claims in help.html, settings.html, and the move-kit message.

verdicts.title: Help FAQ claims the breach check sends no personal information, but the email check sends the email address to HIBP
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced: help.html lines 13-23 answer 'Is my information being sent anywhere?' with 'Neither sends your personal information anywhere' after naming the Breaches page as one of the two exceptions. services/hibp.py check_email (lines 96-113) transmits the full email address in the request URL to haveibeenpwned.com, and hibp.py's own docstring (lines 14-17) plus breaches.html lines 55-59 ('Fair warning: this one does send the email address') both state so. The 'Check the Whole Family at Once' button (breaches.html:75-77) runs that lookup for every stored family email. This is exactly the priority-3 concern ('nothing is sent anywhere' vs the code) with a real, if bounded, priority-1 component: email addresses actually leave the machine after the user relied on a page saying they never do. Medium is right — the transmission only happens if the user bought and configured an HIBP key, and the honest disclosure does exist on the Breaches page itself; the defect is the trusted Help page flatly contradicting it.
verdicts.fix: Reword the help.html FAQ to match breaches.html and hibp.py: the password check sends only the first five characters of a local hash, never the password; the email check does send the address itself (there is no way to ask otherwise), runs only when the user has configured their own paid HIBP key, and only when a Check button is pressed.

verdicts.title: The 'What This App Sends Over the Internet' list is presented as complete but omits the Sources link check and HIBP key validation
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced: settings.html:171 claims 'Nothing, unless you use the Breaches page', yet POST /sources/check (routes/dashboard.py:165-198) fetches all registry URLs via linkcheck.check_links, and save_hibp_key (routes/settings_routes.py:172) calls hibp.verify_key (hibp.py:162-183), which POSTs the key to HIBP's subscription endpoint before saving — from the Settings page itself, directly below the claim. The same exclusivity error appears in breaches.html:8 ('the one part of Identilock that talks to the internet'), setup.html:84 ('The one thing it can look up on the internet'), and hibp.py's docstring line 3. Each network feature is honestly disclosed on its own page (sources.html:44-46 and the settings key hint at line 134), and neither omitted path transmits personal data — the link checker sends bare page requests and key validation sends only the key back to its issuer — so no confidentiality harm. But 'nothing is sent anywhere' claims are the audit's named priority-3 example, and every global summary claiming completeness is provably false in an app whose pitch is auditable honesty. Medium reflects a real, demonstrable honesty defect with no data-leak consequence.
verdicts.fix: Amend the settings.html list to enumerate all network paths: breach checks (password k-anonymity, email lookups), the Sources page 'Check All Links Now' button (plain fetches of the cited agency pages), and HIBP key validation at save time. Change breaches.html's 'the one part' and setup.html's 'the one thing' (and hibp.py's docstring) to accurate phrasing mirroring help.html, which already names the link checker as a second exception.

verdicts.title: Uploaded credit reports over 1MB are spooled to a plaintext temp file on disk despite the 'never written to disk' claim
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced against the installed Starlette in .venv: MultiPartParser creates SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=spool_max_size) with spool_max_size = 1MB for every file part (formparsers.py:147, 230), and the max_part_size guard in on_part_data applies only to non-file parts (the file branch appends to _file_parts_to_write with no size check), so file parts larger than 1MB roll over to a real temp file in the OS temp directory. This happens during form parsing, before the handler's upload.read() and before the MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (25MB) check in reports.py:73 can reject anything. Bureau PDFs routinely exceed 1MB, so the full plaintext report — SSN, accounts, addresses — is written unencrypted to disk on upload; the unlinked file's blocks persist and are forensically recoverable. crypto.py's threat model explicitly includes 'stolen laptop', so this is in scope, and audit priority 1 names 'temp files' as the exact confidentiality question — which is why I raised this from medium to high: the leaked content is the most sensitive data the app handles, the code comment at reports.py:90 and the reports.html:61 hint both assert the opposite, and the leak requires no user mistake. The /setup/import path uses the same mechanism but spools an already-encrypted vault, so it is not a disclosure.
verdicts.fix: Bypass the spooled parser for this route: stream request.body()/request.stream() into an in-memory buffer with an incremental MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES cap and parse the multipart body in memory, or configure the parse with a spool threshold above MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES so the part never leaves RAM (e.g. call request.form() with a raised spool size where the installed Starlette allows, or subclass the parser). At minimum, correct the reports.py comment and the reports.html claim so they match actual behavior, and note the temp-file exposure.

verdicts.title: Green light says address 'checked against the agency's own paperwork', but TransUnion's address was only verified against a third-party page
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced: agency_detail.html:73-74 renders '✓ checked against the agency's own paperwork' for any agency with address_verified, and seeds.py:218 shows TransUnion's mail_address citation is solely 'ca-ag-child-freeze' — the California Attorney General's page (sources.py:112-118, publisher 'California Attorney General', kind 'government', status 'fetched'). A grep across seeds.py confirms TransUnion is the only address_verified agency whose mail_address lacks an own-organization citation: Equifax, Experian, Innovis, LexisNexis, ChexSystems, and NCTUE all cite the organization's own documents. The verification itself is honest (the CA AG page was genuinely fetched), but the tag's specific factual claim is literally false for this row — and green 'verified' lights are the audit's named priority-3 example. Medium rather than low because this tag gates trust on the exact packet containing a child's birth certificate and SSN card, and the failure mode (TransUnion moves its protected-consumer box while the still-alive CA AG page goes stale, keeping every light green) requires no attacker; the adjacent 'still compare it with their site' caveat softens but does not cure a false statement of provenance.
verdicts.fix: Make the tag wording follow the citation's publisher: render 'checked against the agency's own paperwork' only when the mail_address citation includes a source published by the agency itself; otherwise render something like 'confirmed at a government source (California Attorney General), read on DATE'. Alternatively, re-verify TransUnion's protected-consumer mailing address against a TransUnion-published document, add that source to the registry as fetched, and cite it.

verdicts.title: Link-checker's 'alive' result reuses the same green verified tag styling as 'read on DATE', inviting conflation
verdicts.reasoning: Reproduced: sources.html:71 renders '✓ alive' with class src-primary — the identical class and checkmark used at line 62 for '✓ read DATE'. The legend at the top of the page (lines 13-28) explicitly teaches that this green tag means 'a person actually opened this page on that date and copied the facts straight out of it', a meaning the liveness probe does not carry (linkcheck's own messaging in dashboard.py concedes a working link 'doesn't mean the address is wrong — it means nobody can currently confirm it'... i.e. liveness is not verification, and sources.html:43-44 says 'a working link proves the page is there, not that it still says the same thing'). The distinction survives only in a title-attribute tooltip, which the non-technical target audience will rarely hover. Real but low: it is a visual-semantics issue in a separate table column, the correct explanation exists in prose on the same page, and no false statement is rendered — 'alive' is accurate text, just wrongly colored per the page's own color contract.
verdicts.fix: Give the link-check result its own neutral badge style (e.g. a grey or blue src-alive class reading '✓ answers') so green src-primary remains reserved for the human-verified meaning the legend defines, and optionally add a third legend line explaining the Link column's badge.

verdicts.title: Uploaded credit reports over 1MB are written to a cleartext OS temp file, contradicting the code's own claim
verdicts.failure_scenario: User uploads a >1MB credit report PDF on /reports. Starlette's MultiPartParser (installed version 1.3.1, formparsers.py:230) writes the file part into SpooledTemporaryFile(max_size=1MB), which rolls over to a real file in the OS temp directory in cleartext; the max_part_size guard at formparsers.py:184 explicitly applies only to non-file parts. The temp file is unlinked after the request, but the plaintext blocks remain recoverable from the stolen disk, and the file can persist outright if the process dies mid-request.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified directly in the installed Starlette source: spool_max_size is a 1MB class attribute, file parts bypass the 1MB max_part_size check, and nothing in identilock/ overrides MultiPartParser. Credit report PDFs routinely exceed 1MB and contain SSNs/DOBs/account numbers. This sits squarely in priority 1 (cleartext sensitive data to disk, recoverable after laptop theft) and priority 3 (the comment at reports.py:90-91 claiming 'The uploaded file itself is never written to disk' is false for >1MB uploads). The same spooling hits /setup/import but that payload is already encrypted, so the reports path is the real exposure.
verdicts.fix: In create_app (identilock/web.py), before including routers: `from starlette.formparsers import MultiPartParser; MultiPartParser.spool_max_size = 25 * 1024 * 1024` (match MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES so parts stay in RAM), with a test asserting the installed Starlette honors the attribute. Correct the reports.py:90-91 comment and any matching UI copy until then.

verdicts.title: Catastrophic quadratic regex in HTML upload stripping hangs the server indefinitely
verdicts.failure_scenario: A user uploads an HTML file (e.g. a fake 'credit report.html' from a phishing email) containing thousands of unclosed <script> tags with '<html' in the first 2000 chars. The re.sub at reportdiff.py:106 runs O(n^2): measured in this repo's venv at 10s for just 16,000 tags (~128KB), doubling input quadruples time, so a multi-MB file under the 25MB cap runs for days. Because extract_text is called directly inside `async def report_upload` (reports.py:77), it blocks the asyncio event loop itself — a single upload freezes the entire app, including /lock, until the process is killed.
verdicts.reasoning: Empirically reproduced the quadratic scaling (0.16s/0.63s/2.5s/10.1s for 2k/4k/8k/16k tags). Each failed lazy match of `<(script|style)[^>]*>.*?</\1>` under re.S scans to end-of-input. The finding is actually slightly understated: report_upload is an async handler, so the parse blocks the event loop, not a threadpool worker — one request hangs everything, no retry accumulation needed. Denial-of-service only (no data loss; restart recovers), on a local single-user app, so medium is the right ceiling.
verdicts.fix: Make the pattern linear by allowing end-of-input as a closer: r"<(script|style)[^>]*>.*?(?:</\1\s*>|\Z)" — or strip tags with html.parser instead of regex. Additionally, since extract_text runs in an async handler, either make report_upload delegate parsing via run_in_threadpool or convert the parse call accordingly, and consider a much smaller cap for non-PDF uploads.

verdicts.title: pypdf text extraction is unbounded: compression-bomb PDFs can exhaust memory despite the 25MB cap
verdicts.failure_scenario: A crafted PDF within the 25MB cap containing hundreds of content streams, each decompressing to just under pypdf's 75MB per-stream limit (a highly repetitive stream compresses ~1000:1, so ~75KB each), yields multi-GB aggregate extraction: '\n'.join accumulates every page's text with no page-count, total-size, or time budget, driving the process toward OOM or a multi-minute stall. In the milder case, a legitimate-but-huge text extraction (also reachable via plain .txt uploads, which have no post-decode cap) is encrypted and stored whole by save_report, permanently bloating identilock.db, its backups, and every report_detail render.
verdicts.reasoning: The cited code is exactly as described: no page, output, or time bounds, and the full text is persisted. One material correction to the claim: pypdf 6.14.2 (installed) caps each stream at ZLIB_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH = 75,000,000 bytes and raises LimitReachedError beyond it (filters.py:80,92), which report_upload's broad `except Exception` turns into a friendly error — so a single-stream several-GB bomb is already mitigated. The aggregate multi-stream variant and the DB-bloat path survive, which is why this stays confirmed but at low severity: it requires the user to upload a malicious file, and the worst case is DoS/bloat, not disclosure.
verdicts.fix: Inside _extract_pdf, refuse readers with more than ~500 pages, accumulate page text in a loop with a running total capped at ~5MB, and stop early with a visible 'report text truncated' notice; apply the same total-size cap to the non-PDF text path before storage.

verdicts.title: /setup/import has no CSRF or origin check and no size cap, letting a web page plant a vault before first setup
verdicts.failure_scenario: A coworker installs the app but browses the web before completing setup. A malicious page auto-submits a hidden top-level form POST to http://127.0.0.1:8731/setup/import (port is a fixed default, config.py:108) carrying a valid Identilock database keyed to the attacker's passphrase; browsers do not block top-level cross-origin form navigations to loopback. db.is_initialized on the planted file passes, scratch.replace installs it, and the user now sees an unlock screen for a vault whose passphrase the attacker knows. Separately, `await upload.read()` plus `scratch.write_bytes(data)` has no size cap, so a multi-GB POST exhausts RAM/disk.
verdicts.reasoning: Verified: no Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site check exists anywhere in the codebase (only CSP response headers, which do not constrain inbound cross-origin posts), setup_import has no CSRF token (no session exists pre-setup), and the write path is uncapped unlike /reports. The window is genuinely narrow — only before setup completes, exactly the giveaway-to-non-technical-coworkers scenario — and the payoff requires further social engineering to matter, so low is right. This is in-scope local attack surface (priority 4), not the out-of-scope malware case: the attacker is a web page, not code running as the user.
verdicts.fix: At the top of setup_import (and as defense in depth for /setup, /unlock, /recover): reject unless the Origin header is absent or matches request.base_url's host, or Sec-Fetch-Site is 'same-origin'/'none'. Enforce a size cap (e.g. 64MB) on the import body before writing the scratch file.

verdicts.title: str.isdigit()/int() mismatch and unbounded integers turn junk IDs into 500s instead of clean rejections
verdicts.failure_scenario: POST /breaches/email with person_id='²' while unlocked: '²'.isdigit() is True (verified in this venv) so int('²') raises ValueError after the HIBP API call already succeeded — the user gets a bare 500 and the paid lookup result is never saved. person_id='9'*25 passes both guards, then sqlite3.OverflowError ('Python int too large to convert to SQLite INTEGER', verified) fires at bind time; the same overflow turns GET /people/99999999999999999999999999 into a 500 instead of a 404. letters.py:41-43 and reminders.py:67 share the pattern.
verdicts.reasoning: Both failure modes reproduced empirically in the project's venv, and all three cited call sites confirmed in the code. web.py's exception handler covers only HTTPException, so ValueError/OverflowError surface as raw 500s. Severity is correctly low: this is a robustness/UX defect in a single-user local app — no data exposure or corruption — with the worst concrete cost being a lost HIBP lookup result and confusing error pages.
verdicts.fix: Add a helper, e.g. `def parse_id(value: str) -> int | None: try: n = int(value); except ValueError: return None; return n if 0 < n < 2**63 else None`, and use it at breaches.py:76, letters.py:41, and reminders.py:67. For path parameters, declare bounds (Path(..., gt=0, lt=2**63)) or add an OverflowError handler returning 404.

verdicts.title: freeze_save does not verify the person/agency exist, so a stale or forged ID yields a 500 via FOREIGN KEY IntegrityError
verdicts.failure_scenario: User opens a freeze detail form in one tab, deletes that family member in another tab, then submits the form. freeze_save calls update_freeze_record, whose first step ensure_freeze_records (repo.py:374) INSERTs placeholder freeze_records rows for the now-deleted person_id; with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (db.py:189) SQLite raises sqlite3.IntegrityError, no handler catches it (web.py handles only HTTPException), and the user sees an unhandled 500 instead of a 404 or friendly message.
verdicts.reasoning: Confirmed by reading the full chain: freeze_save checks only the status value, unlike its GET counterpart and the letters routes which verify existence first; ensure_freeze_records unconditionally inserts with the supplied person_id under enforced foreign keys. The failure requires a stale tab or hand-crafted request, is purely a UX-level crash with no data loss or exposure, and self-heals on the next valid request — low severity is right for a single-user local app.
verdicts.fix: At the top of freeze_save, mirror the existing pattern from freeze_detail/letter routes: `if get_person(conn, vault, person_id) is None or get_agency(conn, agency_id) is None: raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="No such person or agency.")`.
